{{short description|Statistics on rape and other sexual assaults}}
{{Use Oxford spelling|date=July 2019}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=July 2019}}

{{See also|Estimates of sexual violence#Rape}}{{Rape}}
'''Statistics on rape''' and other acts of [[sexual assault]] are commonly available in [[Developed country|industrialized countries]], and have become better documented throughout the world. Inconsistent [[Rape#Definitions|definitions of rape]], different rates of reporting, recording, prosecution and conviction for [[rape]] can create controversial statistical disparities, and lead to accusations that many rape statistics are unreliable or misleading.<ref name="Gordon2002">{{cite book|author=L. P. Gordon|title=Violence Against Women|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=rmXf-lSuqcgC|year=2002|publisher=Nova Publishers|isbn=978-1-59033-455-3|pages=[https://books.google.com/books?id=rmXf-lSuqcgC&pg=PA4 4–6]}}</ref><ref name=TCJ />

In some jurisdictions, male-on-female rape is the only form of rape counted in the statistics.<ref name=TCJ>{{cite web|url=http://www.cjonline.com/stories/080804/loc_crimestats.shtml |title=Statistics can be misleading |publisher=CJOnline.com |date=8 August 2004 |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref> Some jurisdictions also don't count being forced to penetrate another as rape, creating further controversy around rape statistics.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Sexual Victimisation of Men in America: New Data Challenge Old Assumptions|date=13 May 2014|journal=American Journal of Public Health|doi=10.2105/AJPH.2014.301946 |last1=Stemple |first1=Lara |last2=Meyer |first2=Ilan H. |volume=104 |issue=6 |pages=e19–e26 |pmid=24825225 |pmc=4062022 }}</ref> Countries may not define [[marital rape]] (forced sex on a spouse) as rape.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gangoli |first1=Geetanjali |title=SIX Controlling women's sexuality: rape law in India |chapter=Controlling women's sexuality |date=2011 |publisher=Bristol University Press |page=104 |doi=10.2307/j.ctt9qgkd6.9 |jstor=j.ctt9qgkd6.9 |url=https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/output/1651229 }}</ref> Rape is an [[Under-reporting#Crime|under-reported]] crime. Prevalence of reasons for not reporting rape differ across countries. They may include fear of retaliation, uncertainty about whether a crime was committed or if the offender intended harm, not wanting others to know about the rape, not wanting the offender to get in trouble, fear of prosecution (e.g. due to laws against premarital sex), and doubt in local law enforcement.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Female Victims Of Sexual Violence, 1994-2010|date=7 March 2013|url=http://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=4594|access-date=26 August 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Drug-facilitated, Incapacitated, and Forcible Rape: A National Study|journal=Medical University of South Carolina National Crime Victims Research and Treatment CTR|date=February 2007|page=70}}</ref>

A [[United Nations]] statistical report compiled from government sources showed that more than 250,000 cases of rape or attempted rape were recorded by police annually. The reported data covered 65 countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unodc.org/unodc/en/data-and-analysis/Eighth-United-Nations-Survey-on-Crime-Trends-and-the-Operations-of-Criminal-Justice-Systems.html|title=Eighth United Nations Survey on Crime Trends and the Operations of Criminal Justice Systems |publisher=Unodc.org |date=31 March 2005 |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref>

Most rape research and reporting to date has been limited to male–female forms of rape. Research on male–male and female–male is beginning to be done. However, almost no research has been done on [[Lesbian rape|female–female rape]], though women can be charged with rape in a few jurisdictions. A few books, such as ''Violent Betrayal: Partner Abuse in Lesbian Relationships'' by Dr. Claire M. Renzetti,<ref>Renzetti, Claire M. ''[https://archive.org/details/violentbetrayalp00renz Violent Betrayal: Partner Abuse in Lesbian Relationships]''. Thousand Oaks, CA: Sage Publications, 1992, {{ISBN|0-8039-3888-8}}.</ref> ''No More Secrets: Violence in Lesbian Relationships'' by Janice Ristock,<ref>Ristock, Janice. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=s00oU23jgPMC&q=No+More+Secrets:+Violence+in+Lesbian+Relationships No More Secrets: Violence in Lesbian Relationships]''. New York: Routledge, 2002, {{ISBN|0-415-92946-6}}.</ref> and ''Woman-to-Woman Sexual Violence: Does She Call It Rape?'' by Lori B. Girshick<ref>Girshick, Lori B. ''[https://books.google.com/books?id=nHg40DDZWjAC Woman-to-Woman Sexual Violence: Does She Call It Rape?] (The Northeastern Series on Gender, Crime, and the Law)''. Boston: Northeastern University Press, 2000, {{ISBN|1-55553-527-5}}.</ref> also cover the topic of rape of women by other women.

==By country==
This table indicates the annual number of recorded rapes per capita by country for last available year.<ref name="f967">{{cite web | title=United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, crime-violent-offences | url=https://dataunodc.un.org/crime-violent-offences | access-date=18 May 2025}}</ref> Each entry is based on that country's definition of rape, which varies widely throughout the world. It does not specify whether recorded means reported, brought to trial, or convicted. It does not include cases of rape which go unreported or unrecorded.<ref name=autogenerated1 /><ref name=undata>{{cite web|url=http://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/statistics/crime/CTS12_Sexual_violence.xls |title=UNODC - United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime - Statistics : Crime: Sexual Violence (see second tab of spreadsheet) |publisher=Unodc.org |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref> Alternative estimates can show large differences, such as [[South Africa]] having around 500,000 rapes per year,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.irinnews.org/report/84909/south-africa-one-in-four-men-rape |title=SOUTH AFRICA: One in four men rape |work=IRINnews |publisher=Irinnews.org |date=18 June 2009 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> or [[Rape in Egypt|Egypt]] having more than 20,000 rapes a year.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.rainn.org/africa/egypt |title=Egypt Updated 20 June |publisher=Rainn.com |access-date=2022-12-04|date=26 April 2022 }}</ref>

==Policy and statistics by country==

===Afghanistan===
{{Main|Rape in Afghanistan}}

Rape in [[Afghanistan]] is a crime which can be legally prosecuted, but in practice it is very rarely reported, because of the immense risks that women face if they report it. In 2011, Afghanistan made international news in regard to the story of a woman who was raped by a man, jailed for adultery, gave birth to a child in jail, and was then subsequently pardoned by president [[Hamid Karzai]], and in the end married the man who raped her.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-16179236 |title=Jailed Afghanistan rape victim Gulnaz is freed |work=BBC News |date=14 December 2011 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.channel4.com/news/gulnaz-afghan-rape-afghanistan-adultery-karzai |title=Gulnaz: the Afghan woman forced to marry her rapist - Channel 4 News |publisher=Channel4.com |date=20 June 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

In 2012, Afghanistan recorded 240 cases of honour killings and 160 cases of rape, but did not distinguish between the two crimes.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.khaama.com/240-cases-of-honor-killing-recorded-in-afghanistan-aihrc-2177 |title=240 cases of honor killing recorded in Afghanistan |newspaper=The Khaama Press News Agency |publisher=Khaama.com |access-date=2013-12-03|date=9 June 2013 |last1=Zada |first1=Ahmad Shah Ghani }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://latinbusinesstoday.com/2013/06/aihrc-400-rape-honor-killings-registered-in-afghanistan-in-2-years/ |title=AIHRC: 400 rape, honor killings registered in Afghanistan in 2 years |work=Latin Business Today |date=10 June 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150214224858/http://latinbusinesstoday.com/2013/06/aihrc-400-rape-honor-killings-registered-in-afghanistan-in-2-years/|archive-date=2015-02-14}}</ref> In 2013, in eastern Ghazni, a man attacked a woman and attempted to rape her, and as a result the relatives of the woman killed both the woman and the man in an honour killing.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.khaama.com/honor-killing-afghan-man-and-woman-killed-in-ghazni-1254 |title=Honor killing: Afghan man and woman killed in Ghazni|newspaper=The Khaama Press News Agency|publisher=Khaama.com |access-date=2013-12-03|date=16 January 2013}}</ref> In Afghanistan, crimes such as adultery, rape and trafficking are often conflated with each other,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cimicweb.org/cmo/afg/Documents/Governance/CFC_AFG_Human_Trafficking_Jan2013.pdf |title=Executive Summary: Human Trafficking and Afghanistan |publisher=Cimicweb.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140104055649/https://www.cimicweb.org/cmo/afg/Documents/Governance/CFC_AFG_Human_Trafficking_Jan2013.pdf |archive-date=4 January 2014 }}</ref> and it is generally not acceptable for a woman and a man to be alone together (unless married or related). If this happens, the response can be very violent: an Afghan medical doctor and his female patient were attacked by an angry mob who threw stones at them after the two were discovered in his private examining room without a chaperon.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2013/06/14/world/asia/afghan-doctor-is-killed.html?_r=0|title=Mob Attacks Afghan Doctor and Female Patient|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2013-12-04|first=Rod|last=Nordland|date=13 June 2013}}</ref> In 2013, the security forces were also alleged to rape children in the country.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theamericanconservative.com/routine-child-rape-by-afghan-police/ |title=Routine Child Rape by Afghan Police |work=The American Conservative |date=10 July 2013 |access-date=2013-07-10}}</ref>

===Algeria===
{{Further|Hassi Messaoud mob attacks against women}}
Article 336 of the Penal Code stipulates that rape is a punishable offence, but does not give a definition of rape, as this is left to the courts. The lack of a clear definition of rape in Algerian law makes it difficult for people to report the act and seek legal remedies.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=26096&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=115|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140318212446/http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=26096&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=115|title=The Secretary General's database on violence against women|date=18 March 2014|archive-date=18 March 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ohchr.org/EN/NewsEvents/Pages/DisplayNews.aspx?NewsID=11844&LangID=E|title=OHCHR -|website=www.ohchr.org}}</ref><ref name="amnesty.org.au">[https://www.amnesty.org.au/news/comments/22931/ Algerian authorities must investigate and prosecute attacks against women – Amnesty International Australia<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110903140432/http://www.amnesty.org.au/news/comments/22931/ |date=3 September 2011 }}</ref>

The [[Hassi Messaoud]] was reported in 2001, 2005, and 2010 to sexually assault, traffic, and abuse women.<ref>{{Cite web|date=November 2014|title=ALGERIA: COMPREHENSIVE REFORMS NEEDED TO END SEXUAL AND GENDER-BASED VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN AND GIRLS|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/mde280102014en.pdf|access-date=3 October 2021|website=[[Amnesty International]] (Australia)|publisher=[[Amnesty International]]|type=PDF}}</ref>

There have been continuous allegations that during the [[Algerian War]] French troops had engaged in acts of [[torture]] and rape against Algerians.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/1108014.stm |work=BBC News |title=France confronts Algeria torture claims |date=9 January 2001}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/1671064.stm |work=BBC News |title=Algerian 'war victim' compensated |date=22 November 2001}}</ref>

===Australia===
Non-consensual sexual penetration is termed "rape" in [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[Queensland]], [[South Australia]], and [[Tasmania]]; "Sexual Assault" in [[New South Wales]]; "Sexual intercourse without consent" in the [[Australian Capital Territory|ACT]] and the [[Northern Territory]]; "Sexual penetration without consent" in [[Western Australia]]. All these offences are gender neutral and applicable in marriage. The laws in [[Australia]] have evolved from the [[English common law]] offence of rape, but have gradually changed, especially in the late 20th century.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.alrc.gov.au/publications/25.%20Sexual%20Offences/%E2%80%98rape%E2%80%99-penetrative-sexual-offence |title='Rape': the penetrative sexual offence |publisher=ALRC |access-date=2013-12-03 |date=11 November 2010 |archive-date=3 April 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190403171833/https://www.alrc.gov.au/publications/25.%20Sexual%20Offences/%E2%80%98rape%E2%80%99-penetrative-sexual-offence }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.alrc.gov.au/publications/24.%20Sexual%20Assault%20and%20Family%20Violence/history-activism-and-legal-change |title=History of activism and legal change |publisher=ALRC |access-date=2013-12-03 |date=10 November 2010 |archive-date=21 September 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130921183511/http://www.alrc.gov.au/publications/24.%20Sexual%20Assault%20and%20Family%20Violence/history-activism-and-legal-change }}</ref>

In Australia the reported rape rate per 100,000 people is relatively high, although it is in a decreasing trend, coming down from 91.6 in 2003<ref name=shmh>S. Harrendorf, M. Heiskanen, S. Malby, [http://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/Crime-statistics/International_Statistics_on_Crime_and_Justice.pdf INTERNATIONAL STATISTICS on CRIME AND JUSTICE] United Nations Office on Drugs & Crime (2010)</ref> to 28.6 in 2010.<ref name="nationmaster">{{cite web|url=http://www.nationmaster.com/country-info/stats/Crime/Rape-rate|title=Countries Compared by Crime > Rape rate. International Statistics at NationMaster.com|work=NationMaster.com|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref> This stands in contrast to reported rape rate of 1.2 per 100,000 in [[Japan]], 1.8 per 100,000 in [[India]], 4.6 rapes per 100,000 in [[Bahrain]], 12.3 per 100,000 in [[Mexico]], 24.1 per 100,000 in [[United Kingdom]], 28.6 per 100,000 in [[United States]], 66.5 per 100,000 in [[Sweden]].

During the 12 months prior to interview in 2011–12, an estimated 51,200 (0.3%) Australians aged 18 years and over were a victim of sexual assault. Almost a third (30%) of victims of sexual assault had the most recent incident they experienced reported to the police.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.abs.gov.au/ausstats/abs@.nsf/Lookup/4530.0Chapter2062011-12|title=SEXUAL ASSAULT|access-date=2014-06-22|date=19 February 2013}}</ref>

The Australian Women's Safety Survey conducted by the Bureau of Statistics in 1996 involved a random sample of 6,300 women aged 18 and over. It produced incidence finding of 1.9 per cent for sexual assault in the previous 12 months. Men who are known to the woman accounted for over two-thirds of assailants (68%). Only 15% of the assaulted women in the sample reported to the police.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ausstats.abs.gov.au/Ausstats/subscriber.nsf/0/F16680629C465E03CA256980007C4A81/$File/41280_1996.pdf|title=Women's Safety Australia – 1996 |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref>

===Bangladesh===
{{Main|Rape in Bangladesh}}
[[Bangladesh]] has received criticism for its employment of the "two-finger test" in rape investigations. This test consists of a [[physical examination]] of women who report rape during which a doctor inserts two fingers in the woman's vagina to determine whether the woman is "habituated to sex". This examination has its origin in the country's British colonial-era laws dating back to 1872. This deters many women from reporting rape. More than 100 experts, including doctors, lawyers, police, and women's rights activists, signed a joint statement in 2013 asking for the test, which they called "demeaning", to be abolished, as it "does not provide any evidence that is relevant to proving the offence."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ndtv.com/article/world/bangladesh-activists-urge-ban-on-rape-victim-finger-test-326175 |title=Bangladesh activists urge ban on rape victim 'finger test' |publisher=NDTV.com |date=4 February 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2013/02/05/world/asia/rape-exam-india/index.html |title=Activists: Get rid of 'degrading' parts of India's sexual assault exam |publisher=CNN.com |access-date=2013-12-03 |date=6 February 2013}}</ref> On 12 April 2018 Bangladesh High Court banned the "two-finger test" on the ground that the tests have no scientific merit or evidential value.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.dhakatribune.com/bangladesh/court/2018/04/12/high-court-bans-two-finger-tests-rape/|title=High Court bans 'two finger tests' for rape {{!}} Dhaka Tribune|website=www.dhakatribune.com|language=en-US|access-date=2018-04-29|date=12 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bdnews24.com/bangladesh/2018/04/12/hc-bans-use-of-two-finger-test-bio-manual-test-during-examinations-of-rape-victims|title=HC bans use of 'two-finger test', 'bio-manual test' during examinations of rape victims|website=cess-date=}}</ref>

Between the years of 2010 and 2013, the United Nations Multi-country Study on Men and Violence asked men in rural and urban Bangladesh if they had forced a woman to have sex at any point in their lives. 14.1% of men in rural Bangladesh and 9.5% of men in urban Bangladesh said yes (10% averaged). 2.7% of men in rural Bangladesh and 0.5% (6/1252) in urban Bangladesh had raped in the past year. In rural Bangladesh 41.4% of rapists perpetrated more than once, 3.7% had four or more victims, and 40% first raped as a teenager. 82% of rural Bangladeshi and 79% of urban Bangladeshi men cited entitlement as their reason for rape. 61.2% of urban Bangladeshi men who had raped did not feel guilty or worried afterwards, and 95.1% experienced no legal consequences. 3.7% of men in rural Bangladesh had raped another man. 89.2% of urban Bangladeshi men agreed to the statement "if a woman doesn't physically fight back, it's not rape."<ref name="unwomen-asiapacific.org">{{cite web |url=http://www.undp.org/content/dam/rbap/docs/Research%20%26%20Publications/womens_empowerment/RBAP-Gender-2013-P4P-VAW-Report.pdf |title=Why Do Some Men Use Violence Against Women and How Can We Prevent It? |publisher=UNDP, UNFPA, UN Women and UNV |year=2013 |access-date=26 December 2018 |archive-date=22 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190122125852/http://www.undp.org/content/dam/rbap/docs/Research%20%26%20Publications/womens_empowerment/RBAP-Gender-2013-P4P-VAW-Report.pdf }}<!-- also at https://books.google.com/books?id=ZhGutAEACAAJ --></ref>

===Belgium===
{{Main|Rape in Belgium}}

In 2008, the incidence of rapes recorded by the police was 26.3 per 100,000 people, according to data by [[UNODC]].<ref name="unodc1">[http://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/Crime-statistics/Sexual_violence_sv_against_children_and_rape.xls "Rape at the National Level, number of police recorded offenses".] [[United Nations]].</ref>

Rape in [[Belgium]] is defined by Article 375 of the Penal Code as "any act of sexual penetration, of whatever sort and by whatever means, committed on a non-consenting person".<ref name="ReferenceB">{{cite web|url=http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=10080&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=213|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318212005/http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=10080&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=213|archive-date=18 March 2014|title=The Secretary General's database on violence against women|date=18 March 2014|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref><ref>[http://www.ejustice.just.fgov.be/cgi_loi/loi_a1.pl?DETAIL=1867060801%2FF&caller=list&row_id=1&numero=2&rech=4&cn=1867060801&table_name=LOI&nm=1867060850&la=F&dt=CODE+PENAL&language=fr&fr=f&choix1=ET&choix2=ET&fromtab=loi_all&trier=promulgation&chercher=t&sql=dt+contains++%27CODE%27%26+%27PENAL%27and+actif+%3D+%27Y%27&tri=dd+AS+RANK+&imgcn.x=41&imgcn.y=12 Loi – Wet<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref> Marital rape is also illegal under this law.<ref name="ReferenceB"/>

Apart from criminal proceedings, committing marital rape has also consequences in a [[divorce]] case. The new amendments of the Civil Code regulating marriage and divorce, that came into effect in September 2007, state that any of the spouses, following a divorce, may receive [[alimony]] if they need the money; but a spouse who has committed rape or other violent crimes against the other spouse cannot receive alimony. Article 301 reads: "The court may refuse to grant the application for a alimony if the defendant proves that the applicant has committed a serious offense that rendered it impossible to continue living together. Under no circumstances will alimony be given to a spouse who was found guilty of an act referred to in '''Articles 375''', 398-400, 402, 403 or 405 of the Penal Code, committed against the person of the defendant, or an attempt to commit an act referred to in '''Articles 375''', 393, 394 or 397 of the Code against the same person."<ref>Text in French: "Le tribunal peut refuser de faire droit à la demande de pension si le défendeur prouve que le demandeur a commis une faute grave ayant rendu impossible la poursuite de la vie commune. En aucun cas, la pension alimentaire n'est accordée au conjoint reconnu coupable d'un fait visé aux articles 375, 398 à 400, 402, 403 ou 405 du Code pénal, commis contre la personne du défendeur, ou d'une tentative de commettre un fait visé aux articles 375, 393, 394 ou 397 du même Code contre cette même personne."[http://www.ejustice.just.fgov.be/cgi_loi/loi_a1.pl?DETAIL=1804032130%2FF&caller=list&row_id=1&numero=11&rech=14&cn=1804032130&table_name=LOI&nm=1804032150&la=F&dt=CODE+CIVIL&language=fr&fr=f&choix1=ET&choix2=ET&fromtab=loi_all&trier=promulgation&chercher=t&sql=dt+contains++%27CODE%27%26+%27CIVIL%27and+actif+%3D+%27Y%27&tri=dd+AS+RANK+&imgcn.x=34&imgcn.y=10]</ref>

===Belize===
According to the Belize Police Department, in 2013 there were 26 cases of rape reported in the country.<ref>{{cite news|title=Crime And Violence Statistics Released By Police For 2013|url=http://www.ctv3belizenews.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=4110:crime-and-violence-statistics-released-by-police-for-2013&catid=44:education&Itemid=112|access-date=18 March 2014|date=9 January 2014|publisher=CTV3|archive-date=18 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318093008/http://www.ctv3belizenews.com/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=4110:crime-and-violence-statistics-released-by-police-for-2013&catid=44:education&Itemid=112}}</ref> The estimated total population in 2013 was 334,297.<ref>{{cite web|title=Belize|url=https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/belize/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210109132306/https://www.cia.gov/the-world-factbook/countries/belize|url-status=dead|archive-date=9 January 2021|work=CIA World Factbook|publisher=Central Intelligence Agency|access-date=18 March 2014}}</ref>

In 2006, the incidence of rapes recorded by the police was 15.3 per 100,000 people, according to data by [[UNODC]].<ref name="unodc1" />

According to a 2009 report, [[bribery]] in rape investigations, including those involving child rape, is common. Suspects often offer money to the police or to the victims/their families.<ref>{{cite web |url-status=unfit |url=http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/uploads/Police%20and%20Prosecution%20Training%20Needs-%20Country%20Report.pdf |title=Strengthening State Accountability in Policing and Prosecuting Sexual Assaults |first=Antoinette |last=Moore |date=August 2009 |language=en |access-date=16 August 2023 |website=sgdatabase.unwomen.org |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140319013040/http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/uploads/Police%20and%20Prosecution%20Training%20Needs-%20Country%20Report.pdf |archive-date=19 March 2014}}</ref>{{Full citation needed |date=August 2023}}

The laws were amended in [[Belize]] in 1999 to criminalize marital rape; the law defines marital rape that happens at the time the spouses are cohabiting more narrowly than rape in other circumstances; it stipulates that the act is criminal if "The act of sexual intercourse is preceded or accompanied by or associated with, assault and battery, harm or injury to the female spouse". Rape between unmarried persons, or between separated spouses is defined by lack of consent.<ref>{{cite web|title=s68A(1) of the Criminal Code 1999|url=http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=10088&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=220|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140318104015/http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/searchDetail.action?measureId=10088&baseHREF=country&baseHREFId=220|archive-date=18 March 2014|work=The UN Secretary General's Database on Violence Against Women|publisher=UN Women|access-date=18 March 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=CRIMINAL CODE CHAPTER 101 |url=http://www.oas.org/juridico/mla/en/blz/en_blz-int-text-cc.pdf |publisher=Government of Belize |access-date=10 October 2018 |date=31 December 2000}}</ref>

===Bosnia and Herzegovina===
{{Main|Rape in the Bosnian War}}

During the [[Bosnian war]], rape was prevalent. In 1993, a European Community commission estimated that around 20,000 women were raped, while the Bosnian Government put the figure at 50,000.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/europe/683846.stm |title=EUROPE &#124; Bosnian rape camp trial opens |work=BBC News |date=20 March 2000 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===Botswana===
In a 2009 study, 4.9% of 1244 women of 13–24 years reported having been raped in their lifetimes.<ref>{{cite journal|title= Sexual violence and its health consequences for female children in Swaziland: a cluster survey study| pmid=19428100 | doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(09)60247-6 | volume=373| issue=9679 | journal=Lancet| pages=1966–72 | last1 = Reza | first1 = A | last2 = Breiding | first2 = MJ | last3 = Gulaid | first3 = J | last4 = Mercy | first4 = JA | last5 = Blanton | first5 = C | last6 = Mthethwa | first6 = Z | last7 = Bamrah | first7 = S | last8 = Dahlberg | first8 = LL | last9 = Anderson | first9 = M| year=2009 | s2cid=27933619 | url=https://zenodo.org/record/1259811 | type=Submitted manuscript }}</ref> 10.3% of 654 women reported that they had been raped in their lifetimes in a 2011 study. 4.6% had been raped in the past year. 3.9% of 613 men had been raped in their lifetimes and 4.2% had raped in the past year.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Prevalence and Correlates of Forced Sex Perpetration and Victimization in Botswana and Swaziland |date=31 October 2010 |pmc=3093262 |pmid=21493950 |doi=10.2105/AJPH.2010.300060 |volume=101 |issue=6 |journal=Am J Public Health |pages=1068–74 | last1 = Tsai | first1 = AC | last2 = Leiter | first2 = K | last3 = Heisler | first3 = M | last4 = Iacopino | first4 = V | last5 = Wolfe | first5 = W | last6 = Shannon | first6 = K | last7 = Phaladze | first7 = N | last8 = Hlanze | first8 = Z | last9 = Weiser | first9 = SD}}</ref>

===Brazil===
In Brazil, rape is "alarmingly under-reported" and there are no accurate data to compare rape rates among the country's twenty-six states and federal district.<ref name=f_ortiz>{{cite web |last=Ortiz |first=Fabiola |title=Rape in Brazil Still an Invisible Crime |url=http://www.ipsnews.net/2013/06/rape-in-brazil-still-an-invisible-crime/ |location=Rio de Janeiro, Brazil |publisher=Inter Press Service News Agency |date=24 June 2013|access-date=13 February 2019}}</ref> However, in 2012, there were 6,029 rapes in the [[state of Rio de Janeiro]]; 4,993 of the victims were women.<ref name=f_ortiz /> On average, 416 women a month were raped that year and according to Rio's state [http://www.isp.rj.gov.br/ Institute of Public Security] (ISP) the rate of rape in the state is 37 per 100,000 population for victims of both sexes.<ref name=f_ortiz /> Rio's civil police say that in the first quarter of 2013, 1,822 rapes were committed, while there were only 70 individuals arrested for the crimes. Typically, the victims were mainly black women, aged between 20 and 30 years, and coming from any social class.<ref name=f_ortiz />

===Burma ===
Systematic rape committed by the military against civilians has been documented in Myanmar. A 2002 report by The Shan Human Rights Foundation and The [[Shan Women's Action Network]], titled ''License to Rape'', details incidents of sexual violence committed by [[Tatmadaw]] (Burmese Army) troops in Shan State, mostly between 1996 and 2001.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.burmacampaign.org.uk/reports/License_to_rape.pdf |access-date=23 December 2016 |title=LICENSE TO RAPE |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130730075555/http://www.burmacampaign.org.uk/reports/License_to_rape.pdf |archive-date=30 July 2013}}</ref>

The military of Burma has also been accused of continuing to use rape as a weapon of war after the elections of 2010. In 2014, a women's group, ''The Women's League of Burma'', said it had documented more than 100 cases of rape by the military since 2010.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-25730758|title=Burma military 'using rape as weapon'|journal=BBC News|date=15 January 2014|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=2014-01-15 |title=Accusations of rape as weapon of war in Myanmar |url=https://www.abc.net.au/news/2014-01-15/an-myanmar-military-accused-of-still-using-rape-as-weapon-of-war/5202252 |access-date=2024-08-18 |work=ABC News |language=en-AU}}</ref>

According to a 2012 report by Human Rights Watch, the Burmese security forces have committed killings, rape, and mass arrests against Rohingya Muslims.<ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.hrw.org/reports/2012/08/01/government-could-have-stopped|title=The Government Could Have Stopped This|date=31 July 2012|website=HRW.org|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref>

===Burundi===
Marital rape was criminalized in 2009, albeit with a rather symbolic sentence of only 8 days imprisonment and a fine of 10.000 to 50.000 Fbu.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.oenz.de/fileadmin/users/oenz/PDF/Berichte_OENZ/UPR_BURUNDI_submission_by_OENZ_2012.pdf |title=Joint NGO Submission: UPR on Burundi 15th Session 20134 |publisher=Oenz.de |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=2 April 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150402114730/http://www.oenz.de/fileadmin/users/oenz/PDF/Berichte_OENZ/UPR_BURUNDI_submission_by_OENZ_2012.pdf }}</ref> The new 2009 Criminal Code also criminalized homosexuality which was legal before; but it also abolished the [[capital punishment]] in the country, therefore the new Code received mixed reactions from human rights organizations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/news-and-updates/news/burundi-abolishes-death-penalty-bans-homosexuality-20090427 |title=Burundi abolishes the death penalty but bans homosexuality |publisher=Amnesty International |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

A report by [[Amnesty International]] found that rape was very common in [[Burundi]], rarely prosecuted, and that victims faced strong [[social stigma]] and a high risk of reprisal.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://m.es.amnesty.org/uploads/media/Burundi_SVAW_report_-_No_protection_from_rape_in_war_and_peace.pdf |title=Burundi: No protection from rape in war and peace |publisher=M.es.amnesty.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=17 December 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131217213531/http://m.es.amnesty.org/uploads/media/Burundi_SVAW_report_-_No_protection_from_rape_in_war_and_peace.pdf }}</ref>

===Cambodia===
In [[Cambodia]], rape is estimated by local and international NGOs to be common,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.state.gov/g/drl/rls/hrrpt/2009/eap/135988.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100324180847/http://www.state.gov/g/drl/rls/hrrpt/2009/eap/135988.htm |archive-date=24 March 2010 |title=2009 Human Rights Report: Cambodia|publisher=State.gov |date=11 March 2010 |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref> but only a very small minority of these assaults are ever reported to authorities, due to the social stigma associated to being the victim of a sexual crime, and, in particular, to losing [[virginity]] before [[marriage]] (regardless of how this happened).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.radioaustralia.net.au/connectasia/stories/201003/s2840482.htm |title=Connect Asia:Story:Amnesty calls on Cambodian government to act on rape |publisher=Radio Australia |date=9 March 2010 |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref> From November 2008 to November 2009, police had recorded 468 cases of rape, attempted rape and sexual harassment, a 2.4 percent increase over the previous year.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ipsnews.net/news.asp?idnews=50602 |title=CAMBODIA: Rape Victims Need Better Protection from New Penal Code |publisher=Ipsnews.net |date=9 March 2010 |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref> ''Breaking the Silence&nbsp;– Sexual Violence in Cambodia'' is a report produced by [[Amnesty International]], and released in 2010, which examined the situation of sexual violence in Cambodia. The report found that, in the small minority of rapes which are reported, a very common response is for law-enforcement officials, including
police and court staff, to arrange extralegal out-of-court 'agreements' between the victim and the perpetrator (or their families), in which the rapist pays a sum of money which is shared between the authorities and the victim (and her family), after which the victim has to withdraw any criminal complaint against the perpetrator, and public prosecutors close the case. When a rape is investigated, a complainant is generally expected to pay an extralegal sum of money to the authorities, to ensure that the court investigates the case, otherwise progress is slow, and it may take over two years for anything to happen. During the pre-trial period, there is always a risk that the perpetrator's family will pay a bribe to secure his acquittal or reduced charge.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/asa23/001/2010/en/ |title=BREAKING THE SILENCE&nbsp;— SEXUAL VIOLENCE IN CAMBODIA |date=8 March 2010 |format=PDF |access-date=2010-12-31 }}</ref>

The UN reported results in 2013 from a study that they did in six Asia-Pacific countries about violence against women. 20.4% of Cambodian men said that they had raped a woman in their lifetime and 11.3% had raped in the past year. 3.3% had raped another man at some point and 23% had participated in gang rape, the largest percentage out of the nine areas surveyed. Cambodia was the only area where gang rape was the most commonly reported form of non-partner rape. 45% answered that sexual entitlement was their motive for raping a woman and 42% said they raped to punish a woman. 11.7% of rapists had raped 4 or more women. 52% first perpetrated rape as teenagers and 15.8% first did so under the age of 15. 44.5% of rapists experienced no legal consequences.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://asia-pacific.undp.org/content/dam/rbap/docs/Research%20%26%20Publications/womens_empowerment/RBAP-Gender-2013-P4P-VAW-Report.pdf |title=Why Do Some Men Use Violence Against Women and How Can We Prevent It? |publisher=Asia-pacific.undp.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=28 November 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131128154215/http://asia-pacific.undp.org/content/dam/rbap/docs/Research%20%26%20Publications/womens_empowerment/RBAP-Gender-2013-P4P-VAW-Report.pdf }}</ref>

===Canada===
In [[Former colonies and territories in Canada|Canadian colonies]], rape was an offence at [[common law]]. The conceptualization of rape was based on English common law understanding of this offence. English legal precedent was very important. [[Canada]] got its first statutory definition of rape in 1892, under the 1892 Criminal Code, which read: "Rape is the act of a man having carnal knowledge of a woman who is not his wife without her consent, or with consent which has been extorted by threats or fear of bodily harm, or obtained by personating the woman's husband, or by false and fraudulent representations as to the nature and quality of the act." A boy under 14 could not be convicted of rape.<ref name="constancebackhouse.ca">{{cite web|url=http://www.constancebackhouse.ca/fileadmin/website/rape.htm |title=Rape and Attempt to Commit Rape |publisher=Constancebackhouse.ca |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>
The rape law remained virtually unchanged until 1983, when the criminal offence of "rape" was abolished and replaced by three [[sexual assault]] offences. Unlike the previous rape offence, the sexual assault offences are applicable in [[marriage]] and are gender neutral.<ref name="constancebackhouse.ca"/><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.statcan.gc.ca/pub/85f0033m/85f0033m2008019-eng.pdf |title=Sexual Assault in Canada 2004 and 2007 |publisher=Statcan.gc.ca |access-date=2013-12-03|date=October 2018 }}</ref> These three offences are:
* Sexual assault
* Sexual assault with a weapon, threats to a third party or causing bodily harm
* Aggravated sexual assault.

The most frequently cited research on sexual violence was conducted by [[Statistics Canada]] in 1992, which involved a national random sample of 12,300 women (Johnson and Sacco, 1995). The research found that over one in three women had experienced a sexual assault and that only 6% of sexual assaults were reported to the police.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Johnson | first1 = H. | last2 = Sacco | first2 = V. | year = 1995 | title = Researching violence against women: Statistics Canada's national study | journal = Canadian Journal of Criminology | volume = 37 | issue = 3| pages=281–304| doi = 10.3138/cjcrim.37.3.281 }}</ref> According to Justice Institute of British Columbia, one out of every 17 women is raped, 62% of rape victims were physically injured, 9% were beaten or disfigured.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.assaultcare.ca/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=49&Itemid=58 |title=Statistics of Sexual Assault in Canada |publisher=Rape Victims Support Network |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===China===
{{Main|Rape in China}}

Between the years of 2010 and 2013, the United Nations multi-country Study on Men and Violence in Asia and the Pacific asked men in urban and rural areas of China if they had ever forced a female to have sex. 22.2% said yes. 9.3% had done so in the past year. 55% of the men who had raped had done so more than once and 23.2% had raped more than one woman. 86% cited sexual entitlement as their motive, 57% said that they raped out of fun or boredom, and 46% out of anger or punishment. And despite 47% of them reporting consequences of punishment, threats or violence as a result, 72.4% had not experienced legal consequences. 1.7% had raped another man. 2.2% had participated in gang rape. 25% who had raped reported first doing so as a teenager, the lowest percentage in the study. And while only 11.8% of men and 10.2% of women surveyed approved of generally [[victim blaming|blaming the victim]], 53.7% and 53.5% of each agreed with the statement "if a woman doesn't physically fight back, it's not rape."<ref name="unwomen-asiapacific.org"/>

According to the US Department of State, there were 31,833 cases of rape in China in 2007.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.uschina.usc.edu/w_usci/showarticle.aspx?articleID=13037&AspxAutoDetectCookieSupport=1 |title=Rape in China, University of Southern California |date=7 May 2009 |publisher=Uschina.usc.edu |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===Colombia===
The [[Colombian conflict (1964–present)|armed conflict]] in [[Colombia]] has resulted in increased sexual violence against women; and Colombian authorities have been accused of failing to investigate rape complaints and failing to control sexual attacks in the country.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/news/colombian-authorities-fail-stop-or-punish-sexual-violence-against-women-2012-10-04 |title=Colombian authorities fail to stop or punish sexual violence against women |publisher=Amnesty International |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Marital rape was criminalized in 1996.<ref name="omct.org">{{cite web|url=http://www.omct.org/files/2004/07/2409/eng_2003_04_colombia.pdf |title=Violence against Women in Colombia |publisher=Omct.org |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Rape is very common among internally displaced women: it is reported that one in five of these women were raped.<ref name="omct.org"/>

===Democratic Republic of the Congo===
{{Main|Sexual violence in the Democratic Republic of the Congo}}

[[File:DRC raped women.jpg|thumb|Meeting of victims of sexual violence in the Democratic Republic of the Congo]]
In eastern Congo, the prevalence and intensity of rape and other sexual violence is described as the worst in the world.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/09/08/AR2007090801194.html|title=Prevalence of Rape in E.Congo Described as Worst in World |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=9 September 2007|access-date=2010-12-31 |first=Stephanie |last=McCrummen}}</ref> It is estimated that there are as many as 200,000 surviving rape victims living in the Democratic Republic of the Congo today.<ref name="film.guardian.co.uk">{{cite news|author=Kira Cochrane|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2008/may/09/women.congo |title=Kira Cochrane talks to filmmaker Lisa F Jackson on her documentary about rape in the Congo |publisher=Film.guardian.co.uk |date= 9 May 2008|access-date=2010-12-31|location=London}}</ref><ref name="pbs.org">{{cite web|url=https://www.pbs.org/pov/pov2007/lumo/special_ensler.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080110221137/http://www.pbs.org/pov/pov2007/lumo/special_ensler.html |archive-date=10 January 2008 |title=A Conversation with Eve Ensler: Femicide in the Congo |publisher=Pbs.org |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref> A new study says more than 400,000 women are raped in the Democratic Republic of Congo annually.<ref>"[https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world/africa/400000-rapes-in-congo-in-one-year-2283102.html 400,000 rapes in Congo in one year]". The Independent. 12 May 2011.</ref> War rape in the Democratic Republic of Congo has frequently been described as a "weapon of war" by commentators. Louise Nzigire, a local social worker, states that "this violence was designed to exterminate the population." Nzigire observes that rape has been a "cheap, simple weapon for all parties in the war, more easily obtainable than bullets or bombs."
In an analysis of 2565 patients who received medical care in the Médecins Sans Frontières sexual violence clinic in the capital of Ituri, Bunia, between 2005 and 2006, 73% (95.2% of male victims) reported being raped by armed men. 74.5% experienced gang rape (89.3% of male and 73.9% of female victims), with attack by between two and four perpetrators being the most common scenario (58.9%) for both sexes. 48.6% of victims were attacked while doing daily domestic activities outside their homes.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=Description and consequences of sexual violence in Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo |journal=BMC International Health and Human Rights |volume=11 |article-number=5 |doi=10.1186/1472-698X-11-5 |pmid=21504596 |pmc=3108309 |year=2011 |last1=Duroch |first1=Françoise |last2=McRae |first2=Melissa |last3=Grais |first3=Rebecca F. |doi-access=free }}</ref>

===Denmark===
Although only approximately 500 rapes are reported to the Danish police annually, several studies estimate that only a small minority of all rapes are actually reported, and only one in five reported rapes result in a conviction in court.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tal og fakta om voldtægt|url=http://www.amnesty.dk/side/tal-og-fakta-om-voldtaegt|publisher=[[Amnesty International]]|access-date=13 October 2014|language=da|archive-date=18 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141018040601/http://www.amnesty.dk/side/tal-og-fakta-om-voldtaegt}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Voldtægt|url=http://www.dkr.dk/voldt%C3%A6gt-0|publisher=Danish Crime Prevention Council|access-date=13 October 2014|language=da|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141026122634/http://www.dkr.dk/voldt%C3%A6gt-0|archive-date=26 October 2014}}</ref> For example, according to a 2014 study published by the [[Fundamental Rights Agency|European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights]], Denmark had the highest prevalence rate of physical and sexual violence against women in Europe.<ref>{{cite web|title=A third of women in EU have suffered 'sexual violence'|url=http://www.france24.com/en/20140305-one-third-women-eu-victims-sexual-violence-crime-rape/|publisher=[[France 24]]|access-date=13 October 2014|date=5 March 2014}}</ref><ref name="EU-study">{{cite web|title=Violence against women: an EU-wide survey|url=http://fra.europa.eu/sites/default/files/fra-2014-vaw-survey-main-results_en.pdf|publisher=[[European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights]]|access-date=14 May 2014|pages=28–30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140307224554/http://fra.europa.eu/sites/default/files/fra-2014-vaw-survey-main-results_en.pdf|archive-date=7 March 2014}}</ref>

The Danish government was harshly criticized for inadequate laws in regard to sexual violence in a 2008 report produced by [[Amnesty International]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/act77/001/2010/en/ |title=Case Closed: Rape and Human Rights in the Nordic Countries, Summary Report |date=8 March 2010 |publisher=[[Amnesty International]] |access-date=2013-02-03 }}</ref> The Danish criminal provisions regarding sexual crimes had remained nearly unchanged for 30 years, which lead Amnesty International to declare that "legislation on rape and sexual violence [conflicted] with human rights principles concerning the need to protect an individual's sexual and physical integrity and right to self-determination."<ref name="caseclosed">{{cite web|title=Case Closed |url=http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |publisher=[[Amnesty International]] |access-date=13 October 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020202147/http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |archive-date=20 October 2013 }}</ref> The organization repeatedly urged Denmark to bring legislation on rape in line with international law over several years,<ref>{{cite press release|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur18/001/2011/en/ |title=Amnesty International Public Statement |publisher=Amnesty International |date=23 September 2011 |access-date=2013-02-03 }}</ref> which lead to an amendment to the sexual offences code in 2013, following a change in government after the [[2011 Danish general election|2011 elections]].<ref name="ReferenceC">{{cite web|url=http://www.amnesty.dk/nyhed/amnesty/ny-voldtaegtslovgivning-er-en-sejr-danske-kvinders-retssikkerhed|title=Ny voldtægtslovgivning er en sejr for danske kvinders retssikkerhed|language=da|publisher=[[Amnesty International]]|access-date=24 April 2014|archive-date=2 July 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150702182036/http://www.amnesty.dk/nyhed/amnesty/ny-voldtaegtslovgivning-er-en-sejr-danske-kvinders-retssikkerhed}}</ref><ref name="konerabat">{{cite news|title=Slut med 'konerabat' for voldtægt|url=http://www.b.dk/nationalt/slut-med-konerabat-for-voldtaegt|newspaper=Berlingske|access-date=13 October 2014|language=da|date=3 June 2013}}</ref>

Sexual offences ({{langx|da|Seksualforbrydelser}}) are defined in the [[Danish Penal Code]], Chapter 24, Section 216–236. References in legislation to marriage were removed following the 2013 amendment (previously providing for a reduced sentence or a pardon),<ref name="caseclosed" /> and sexual acts performed on victims in a helpless state now also count as rape.<ref name="konerabat" /><ref name="themis.dk">{{cite web|title=Straffeloven|url=http://www.themis.dk/synopsis/index.asp?hovedramme=/synopsis/docs/lovsamling/straffeloven_indholdsfortegnelse.html|language=da}}</ref>

In Denmark it was only 1999 that the first [[rape crisis centre]] was established.<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160304121227/http://www.nsfk.org/BIBLIOGRAPHY/p/show/BArticleID/5116/Politi--og-ikke-politianmeldt-voldt%C3%A6gt-og-voldt%C3%A6gtsfors%C3%B8g-i-%C3%85rhus-amt-i-perioden-1.-november-1999---1.-november-2000 POLITI- OG IKKE-POLITIANMELDT VOLDTÆGT OG VOLDTÆGTSFORSØG I ÅRHUS AMT I PERIODEN 1. NOVEMBER 1999 - 1. NOVEMBER 2000] (archived from [http://www.nsfk.org/BIBLIOGRAPHY/p/show/BArticleID/5116/Politi--og-ikke-politianmeldt-voldt%C3%A6gt-og-voldt%C3%A6gtsfors%C3%B8g-i-%C3%85rhus-amt-i-perioden-1.-november-1999---1.-november-2000 the original] on 4 March 2016)</ref>

===East Timor===
Marital rape was made illegal in [[East Timor]] in 2010, under the ''Law on Domestic Violence, Law No. 7/2010'' which states that "Sexual violence is understood as any conduct that induces the person to witness, to maintain or participate in unwanted sexual relations, ''even within a marriage'', through intimidation, threats, coercion or use of force, or which limits or nullifies the exercise of sexual and reproductive rights".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ilo.org/wcmsp5/groups/public/---ed_protect/---protrav/---ilo_aids/documents/legaldocument/wcms_179323.pdf |title=Law Against Domestic Violence |publisher=[[International Labour Organization]] |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

The UN claimed that thousands of East Timorese women were raped during the [[Indonesian occupation of East Timor]] and that rape was used by the [[Indonesian military]] as a [[war rape|weapon of war]]. The UN commission stated that: "Rape, sexual slavery and sexual violence were tools used as part of the campaign designed to inflict a deep experience of terror, powerlessness and hopelessness upon pro-independence supporters."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gsp.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/UN%20verdict%20on%20East%20Timor.pdf |title=UN verdict on East Timor |publisher=Yale.edu |date=19 January 2006 |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150528141816/http://gsp.yale.edu/sites/default/files/files/UN%20verdict%20on%20East%20Timor.pdf |archive-date=28 May 2015}}</ref>

===Egypt===
{{Main|Rape in Egypt}}

Marital rape is not a criminal offence in [[Egypt]]. Unlike many other countries in the Middle East, Egypt has, in 1999, abolished the law which stipulated that a man could escape a rape conviction if he married his victim after the fact.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://globalwebpost.com/farooqm/study_res/islam/gender/norman_rape.pdf |title=Democracy and Development: Challenges for the Islamic World |publisher=Globalwebpost.com |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=17 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131017013601/http://globalwebpost.com/farooqm/study_res/islam/gender/norman_rape.pdf }}</ref>

Women are generally fearful when it comes to reporting rape. [[Engy Ghozlan]] of [[Egyptian Centre for Women's Rights]] and others suggest that the number of rape cases is over 200,000 every year. Ghozlan further adds that rapes are not decreasing because young men lack adequate income and employment, so their marriages are delayed.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.irinnews.org/report/76827/egypt-are-attitudes-to-rape-beginning-to-change |title=EGYPT: Are attitudes to rape beginning to change? |work=IRINnews |publisher=Irinnews.org |date=19 February 2008 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

During the [[2012–13 Egyptian protests|2012-13 Egyptian protests]], rape has been carried out publicly. On 3 July 2013, it was reported that about 91 women were raped and sexually abused in [[Tahrir Square]] in four days. By some estimates, the figure was about 169.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.rappler.com/world/32942-women-raped-egypt-protests-human-rights/ |title=At least 169 women raped at Egypt protests |work=Rappler.com |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===Ethiopia===
Rape is a very serious problem in [[Ethiopia]],<ref>{{cite web|url=https://news.yahoo.com/did-west-ignore-rape-charges-related-ethiopia-land-211839133.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20130729134751/http://news.yahoo.com/did-west-ignore-rape-charges-related-ethiopia-land-211839133.html|title=Did West ignore rape charges related to Ethiopia land grab? - Yahoo! …|date=29 July 2013|archive-date=29 July 2013}}</ref> and the country is infamous for the practice of [[marriage by abduction]], with the prevalence of this practice in Ethiopia being one of the highest in the world.<ref>{{cite news|last=Henshaw |first=Amber |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/4763185.stm |title=Ethiopian girls fear forced marriage |work=BBC News |date=14 May 2006 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last=Ross |first=Will |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-13681053 |title=Ethiopian girls fight child marriages |work=BBC News |date=7 June 2011 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.popcouncil.org/pdfs/briefingsheets/ETHIOPIA.pdf |title=Child Marriage Briefing: Ethiopia |publisher=Popcouncil.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=9 August 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110809133219/http://www.popcouncil.org/pdfs/briefingsheets/ETHIOPIA.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.pathfinder.org/publications-tools/pdfs/Causes-and-Consequesnces-of-Early-Marriage-in-the-Amhara-Region-of-Ethiopia.pdf |title=Report on Causes and Consequences of Early Marriage in Amhara Region |publisher=Pathfinder.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130323124732/http://www.pathfinder.org/publications-tools/pdfs/Causes-and-Consequesnces-of-Early-Marriage-in-the-Amhara-Region-of-Ethiopia.pdf |archive-date=23 March 2013 }}</ref> In many parts of Ethiopia, it is common for a man, working in co-ordination with his friends, to kidnap a girl or woman, sometimes using a horse to ease the escape.<ref>BBC, [http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/371944.stm "Ethiopia: Revenge of the Abducted Bride"], 18 June 1999.</ref> The abductor will then hide his intended bride and rape her until she becomes pregnant. As the father of the woman's child, the man can claim her as his wife.<ref name="ReferenceA">BBC, "Ethiopia: Revenge of the Abducted Bride"</ref> Subsequently, the kidnapper may try to negotiate a [[bride price]] with the village elders to legitimize the marriage.<ref name="ReferenceA" /> Girls as young as eleven years old are reported to have been kidnapped for the purpose of marriage.<ref>UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, [http://www.irinnews.org/Report.aspx?ReportId=69993 ''ETHIOPIA: Surviving forced marriage'']</ref>

Ethiopia is estimated to have one of the highest rates of [[violence against women]] in the world. A report by the UN found that women in Ethiopia are the most likely to suffer [[domestic violence]] at the hands of their partners, and that nearly 60% of Ethiopian women were subjected to sexual violence.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/6040180.stm |title=Ethiopian women are most abused |work=BBC News |date=11 October 2006 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> The 2004 Criminal Code of Ethiopia creates the offence of rape, by Article 620, which states that: "Whoever compels a woman to submit to sexual intercourse outside wedlock, whether by the use of violence or grave intimidation, or after having rendered her unconscious or incapable of resistance, is punishable with rigorous imprisonment from five years to fifteen years". There are also certain aggravated circumstances which lead to an increased punishment for rape. Apart from the criminal offence of rape, there are also other sexual offences in the Criminal Code. The [[age of consent]] is 18.<ref name="sgdatabase.unwomen.org">{{cite web|url=http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/uploads/Ethiopia%20-%20Revised%20Criminal%20Code%202004.pdf |title=The Criminal Code of The Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia |publisher=Sgdatabase.unwomen.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222202126/http://sgdatabase.unwomen.org/uploads/Ethiopia%20-%20Revised%20Criminal%20Code%202004.pdf |archive-date=22 February 2014}}</ref> As can be seen above, a woman cannot charge her husband with rape. However, the 2004 Criminal Code brings major improvements for [[women's rights]] in the country, by criminalizing several forms of violence against women, such as [[female genital mutilation]], violence against [[pregnant]] women, marriage by abduction, [[child marriage]], [[Human trafficking|trafficking]] and [[sexual harassment]], though ''Chapter III&nbsp;– Crimes Committed against life, person and health through harmful traditional practices'' (Articles 561–570) and other provisions (Articles 587, 597, 625, 635, 637, 648). Article 564&nbsp;– ''Violence Against a Marriage Partner or a Person Cohabiting in an Irregular Union'' is a major step forward.<ref name="sgdatabase.unwomen.org"/>

The Ethiopian [[military]] has been accused of committing systematic rapes against civilians.<ref name="hrw.org">{{cite web|author1=Leslie Lefkow |author2=deputy Africa director |url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2012/08/28/ethiopia-army-commits-torture-rape |title=Ethiopia: Army Commits Torture, Rape |publisher=Human Rights Watch |date=28 August 2012 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref name="news.bbc.co.uk">{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/4379119.stm |title=Ethiopia army 'killed and raped' |work=BBC News |date=24 March 2005 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Human Rights Watch has repeatedly claimed that the army has attacked, beaten, raped and killed civilians, something which the Ethiopian authorities have denied.<ref name="hrw.org"/><ref name="news.bbc.co.uk"/> However, US scientists said that satellite images confirmed reports that the Ethiopian military had burnt towns and villages in Ethiopia's Somali region.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/7450533.stm |title=Images back Ethiopia abuse claim |work=BBC News |date=12 June 2008 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

A study in [[Addis Ababa]] of high school boys found that 4.3% had been raped in their lives.<ref>{{Cite journal|title=BMC International Health and Human Rights &#124; Full text &#124; Prevalence of sexual abuse of male high school students in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia |journal=BMC International Health and Human Rights |volume=13 |page=24 |doi=10.1186/1472-698X-13-24 |pmid=23680171 |pmc=3682909 |year=2013 |last1=Haile |first1=Rahel Tesfaye |last2=Kebeta |first2=Negussie Deyessa |last3=Kassie |first3=Getnet Mitike |doi-access=free }}</ref> According to the ''WHO Multi-country Study on Women's Health and Domestic Violence against Women'', 59% of women reported sexual abuse by a partner; while one third of women reported being "physically forced" to have sex against their will with their partner within the past 12 months. This was the highest prevalence of all countries surveyed.<ref name="who.int">[https://www.who.int/gender/violence/who_multicountry_study/summary_report/summary_report_English2.pdf?ua=1 WHO Multi-country Study on Women's Health and Domestic Violence against Women - Initial results on prevalence, health outcomes and women's responses] WHO</ref>

===Finland===
{{Main|Sexual violence in Finland}}

In [[Finland]], the legal regulations on sexual offences were revised with a law that came into effect on 1. January 1999. Under this revision, sexual offences were divided into three levels: rape, aggravated rape and forcing someone into a sexual act. The revision also affects the cause of action. The law on rape (Chapter 20 - Sex offences Section 1 - Rape) states that: "(1) A person who forces another into sexual intercourse by the use or threat of violence shall be sentenced for rape to imprisonment for at least one year and at most six years.
(2) Also a person who, by taking advantage of the fact that another person, due to unconsciousness, illness, disability, state of fear or other state of helplessness, is unable to defend himself or herself or to formulate or express his or her will, has sexual intercourse with him or her, shall be sentenced for rape."<ref name=StatTiedotteet>{{cite web|url=https://www.stat.fi/ajk/tiedotteet/v2004/275oiks_tausta-aineisto.pdf|title=Rikollisuustilanne |publisher=Tilastokeskus |year=2004|access-date=11 October 2014}}</ref><ref name=Finlex>{{cite web|url=https://www.finlex.fi/fi/lainsaadanto/1889/39-001|title=Rikoslaki|publisher=Finlex|year=2014|access-date=11 October 2014}}</ref> The Finnish government does not produce data on rape on a regular basis, beyond the raw numbers of reported rape to Finnish police. The laws and guidelines have been criticized for not making specific reference to "consent" and for offering the possibility of [[mediation]] between the victim and perpetrator.<ref name="European Women's Lobby">{{cite web|title=2013 EWL Barometer on Rape - Report|url=http://www.womenlobby.org/spip.php?action=acceder_document&arg=3156&cle=ab1b643179f1c246da5c58170ed9b716248632e0&file=pdf%2F2714_finland_lr.pdf|publisher=European Women's Lobby|access-date=13 October 2014}}</ref> Specific information on women victims of rape can be found only from separate studies, the last one made in 2004,<ref name="European Women's Lobby"/> and that study was based on reported rape offences during the years 1998–1999. The study showed that of 468 rapes or attempted rapes reported to the police, only 47 rape charges were made, or that merely 10 per cent of the rapes reported to the police lead to a prosecution. In most cases the rape victim and the offender knew each other, only in every fourth case was the woman attacked by a stranger. Almost half the rape occurred among acquaintances (corresponding to a [[date rape]]), and intimate or family relations were involved in 13 per cent of the cases.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kainulainen|first1=Heini|title=Raped? A Study of Rape in Criminal Proceedings|url=http://www.optula.om.fi/material/attachments/optula/julkaisut/tutkimuksia-sarja/0SrSnm6gZ/212_Kainulainen_2004.pdf|publisher=The National Research Institute of Legal Policy in Finland|access-date=13 October 2014|language=fi, en|year=2004}}</ref>

Finland had 980 cases of reported rape in 2013.<ref>{{cite web|title=Petosten ja maksuvälinepetosten määrä lisääntyi vuonna 2013|url=http://www.stat.fi/til/polrik/2013/04/polrik_2013_04_2014-01-17_tie_001_fi.html|publisher=Statistics Finland|access-date=13 October 2014|language=fi|date=1 January 2014}}</ref> The number of reported rape had increased in 2006 by 91% when measured since 1977, and by 27% when measured from 1997.<ref name="daphne-study">{{cite book|author1=Jo Lovett|author2=Liz Kelly|title=Different systems, similar outcomes?|url=http://kunskapsbanken.nck.uu.se/nckkb/nck/publik/fil/visa/197/different|publisher=London Metropolitan University|access-date=10 July 2014|year=2009}}</ref> According to a 2014 study published by the [[European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights]], approximately 47% of women surveyed in Finland were said to have suffered physical and/or sexual abuse; which was the second highest rate after Denmark.<ref name="EU-study" /><ref>{{cite web|title=A third of women in EU have suffered 'sexual violence'|url=http://www.france24.com/en/20140305-one-third-women-eu-victims-sexual-violence-crime-rape/|publisher=France 24 with AP & AFP|access-date=14 May 2014|date=5 March 2014}}</ref> Finland was one of the last countries in the EU to criminalize marital rape, making it illegal in 1994, after years of debate.<ref name="amnesty.dk">{{cite web|url=http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |title=Case Closed: Rape and Human Rights in the Nordic Countries |publisher=Amnesty International |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020202147/http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |archive-date=20 October 2013 }}</ref>

Convicted rapists receive very short penalties compared to other countries, although this may be due to the fact that Finland has one of the lowest [[incarceration rate]]s in the world. During 2001–2003, the average sentence for rape was two years' imprisonment, and only 63% of offenders served their sentences in prison, as 37% of sentences were conditional. The average sentence for aggravated rape was four years' imprisonment. For the offence of coercion into sexual intercourse, sentences were most often one year conditional imprisonment, but only 4% of offenders went to prison.<ref name="amnesty.dk"/>

The issue of [[violence against women]] in Finland has been of major international interest and the situation has been described as a [[paradox]], because otherwise the country has offered women high professional and social opportunities.<ref name="academia.edu">{{Cite journal|last=Clarke |first=Kris |url=https://www.academia.edu/992154 |title=The Paradoxical Approach to Intimate Partner Violence in Finland &#124; Kris Clarke |publisher=Academia.edu |date=1 January 1970 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://eprints.hud.ac.uk/6440/|title=Gender-neutrality, gender equality and policy: comparing and contrasting policy responses to 'domestic violence' in Finland and Scotland|pages=85–107|first1=Hearn|last1=Jeff|first2=McKie|last2=Linda|date=18 March 2017|journal=HUD.ac.uk|issue=48|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref> According to Turku University law professor Kevät Nousiainen, "the way Finns conceive gender is different. It's assumed women are perfectly capable of taking care of themselves, and if they are not able to do so, that is unacceptable." After World War I, Finland fought a war of independence, a civil war, and two decades later the Winter War, the Continuation War, and the Lapland War, which made up Finland's part in World War II. In each case Finland fought as a poorly trained underdog in brutal conditions that Nousiainen says left men "unbalanced". "Violence was taken somehow for granted, it was tolerated. And then you have to consider the transfer of violent behaviour from generation to generation," she said.<ref>{{cite web |title=Feminism, war and silence fuel domestic abuse in Finland |url=https://www.dawn.com/news/575185 |website=DAWN.COM |access-date=4 June 2018 |date=23 October 2010}}</ref>

===France===
{{Main|Rape in France}}

Article 222-23 of the criminal code reads: "Any act of sexual penetration, whatever its nature, committed against another person by violence, constraint, threat or surprise, is rape".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.legifrance.gouv.fr/affichCode.do;jsessionid=3199A092657C0E24B4F431E0EFEFA28F.tpdjo14v_1?idSectionTA=LEGISCTA000006181753&cidTexte=LEGITEXT000006070719&dateTexte=20140605|title=Code pénal - Legifrance|work=legifrance.gouv.fr|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref>

===Germany===
{{Main|Rape in Germany}}

Under German law, a person commits rape if they employ any of these three types of coercion: 1. force; or 2. threat of imminent danger to life or limb; or 3. exploitation of a situation in which the victim is unprotected and at the mercy of the offender.<ref name="gesetze-im-internet.de">{{cite web|url=http://www.gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_stgb/index.html |title=German Criminal Code |publisher=Gesetze-im-internet.de |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Germany was one of the last Western countries to criminalize marital rape, it did so only in 1997, after a lengthy political battle which started in the 1970s. The criminalization of marital rape has been delayed by political disagreement: even when there was consensus that it should be criminalized, there was disagreement between those who wanted it punished and prosecuted in the same way as non-marital rape and those who opposed this. These disagreements have delayed the criminalization until 1997, when rape in marriage was made illegal being treated in the same way as non-marital rape.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.jurawelt.com/sunrise/media/mediafiles/13792/tenea_juraweltbd52_kieler.pdf |author=Marita Kieler |title=Tatbestandsprobleme der sexuellen Notigung, Vergewaltigung sowie des sexuellen Mitbrauchs widerstandsunfahiger Personen |publisher=Jurawelt.com |access-date=2013-12-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020164804/http://www.jurawelt.com/sunrise/media/mediafiles/13792/tenea_juraweltbd52_kieler.pdf |archive-date=20 October 2013 }}</ref> In Germany the [[age of consent]] is 14, although some limitations do exist up to the age of 18 (regarding the exploitation of the lack of capacity for sexual self-determination of 14–15 y/o; and engaging in sexual activity with a person under 18 "by taking advantage of an exploitative situation"; or paying for sex with a minor under 18 - ''Section 182'' of the [[Strafgesetzbuch|Criminal Code]]).<ref name="gesetze-im-internet.de"/> Chapter 13 of the Criminal Code is called "''Offences against sexual self-determination''" and consists of Sections 174 to 184 which define sexual crimes.

===Ghana===
In a survey of [[Ghana]]ians, 8% of women reported having been raped by a man in their lifetimes and 5% of men reported having raped a wife or girlfriend.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.un.org/womenwatch/daw/egm/vaw-stat-2005/docs/expert-papers/Ardayfio.pdf |title=Violence against women: a statistical overview, challenges and gaps in data collection and methodology and approaches for overcoming them |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===Iceland===
Rape in [[Iceland]] is defined by Article 194 of the Penal Code which states: "Any person who has sexual intercourse or other sexual relations with a person by means of using violence, threats or other unlawful coercion shall be guilty of rape and shall be imprisoned for a minimum of 1 year and a maximum of 16 years. 'Violence' here refers to the deprivation of independence by means of confinement, drugs or other comparable means. Exploiting a person's psychiatric disorder or other mental handicap, or the fact that, for other reasons, he or she is not in a condition to be able to resist the action or to understand its significance, in order to have sexual intercourse or other sexual relations with him or her, shall also be considered as rape, and shall result in the same punishment as specified in the first paragraph of this article."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://eng.innanrikisraduneyti.is/laws-and-regulations/nr/119|title=Excerpts from the General Penal Code, No. 19/1940, with subsequent amendments. Chapter XXII - Sexual Offences and Chapter XXIII - Homicide and Bodily Harm|work=InnanRikisraduneyti.is|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref>

Although a [[Nordic country]], known for a high level of [[gender equality]], Iceland has, until recently,{{When|date=March 2017}} maintained outdated provisions in its sexual offences laws. Before 2007, the law in regard to rape and certain other sexual offences stated that, if after the assault the victim and the perpetrator got married or entered into an informal cohabitation, then the punishment could be waived; if the assault took place between married or cohabiting partners, and following the act, the victim continued to live together with the perpetrator, then the punishment could also be waived. These provisions were repealed by Act No. 61/2007. Other legal changes which were made included the broadening of the definition of rape and other sexual offences, and the raising of the age of consent to 15, from 14.<ref>http://www.coe.int/t/dghl/monitoring/socialcharter/reporting/statereports/Iceland22_en.pdf The former Article 205, repealed by Act No. 61/2007, stated that "''Penalty under Art. 194–199, 202 and 204 may be dropped if a man and a woman between whom the sexual intimacy has occurred have later entered into wedlock or embarked upon informal co-habitation or if they were married at the time or in informal co-habitation, having thereafter embarked upon continued co-habitation.''" – the text of the Penal Code as it was in the year 2003 can be found here:[http://www.wipo.int/wipolex/en/text.jsp?file_id=190914]</ref>

In 2008, the incidence of rapes recorded by the police was 21.6 per 100,000 people, according to data by [[UNODC]].<ref name="unodc1" /> A 2010 study found that 6% of Icelandic women had been sexually victimized in an intimate relationship during their lifetime.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wave-network.org/sites/default/files/05%20ICELAND%20END%20VERSION.pdf|title=WAVE Network|work=Wave-Network.org|access-date=18 March 2017|archive-date=22 February 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222070702/http://www.wave-network.org/sites/default/files/05%20ICELAND%20END%20VERSION.pdf}}</ref>

===India===
{{Main|Rape in India}}

Based on statistics published by [[Statista]], the country had a rape rate of approximately 2.21 per 100,000 people as of 2022.<ref>{{Cite web |title=India: rape cases 2022 |url=https://www.statista.com/statistics/632493/reported-rape-cases-india/?srsltid=AfmBOopGt2ZUns2oHrPM0D1QQcolCV8QMsh4h9dAJ8eCEdM-_5LyhQh1 |access-date=2025-11-04 |website=Statista |language=en}}</ref> The [[National Crime Records Bureau]] (NCRB) in its 2023 report put India's rape rate at 4.4 per 100,000 ''women''.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |year=2025 |title=Crime in India, Volume I |url=https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/files/1CrimeinIndia2023PartI1.pdf |url-status=live |access-date=10 November 2025 |website=National Crime Records Bureau |page=274 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20251122094502/https://www.ncrb.gov.in/uploads/files/1CrimeinIndia2023PartI1.pdf|archive-date=November 22, 2025}}</ref> However, the incidence of rape and its rates of reporting vary widely from rural to urban areas, and across India's [[States and union territories of India|28 states and 8 union territories]].

In 2018, official data showed that 1 rape was reported every 5 minutes in India. Of the 134,000 cases reported, just over 85 per cent led to charges, and 27 per cent ultimately led to convictions.<ref>{{cite news|title=NCRB data 2018: 1 rape reported every 5 minutes in India|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/india/story/ncrb-2018-woman-reports-rape-every-15-minutes-in-india-1635924-2020-01-11|publisher=indiatoday.in|access-date=27 September 2020}}</ref> Of these, 31,320 were committed by perpetrators known to the victim (93.9% of the cases).<ref>{{cite news|title=Rapes in India: 94% offenders known to victim|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/india/story/rapes-in-india-offenders-victim-minor-data-ncrb-1635691-2020-01-10|website=indiatoday.in|access-date=27 September 2020}}</ref> This had increased to 97.5% by end-2023.<ref name=":2" /> As high as 27.8 per cent of victims were minors or below 18, the legal age of consent.<ref>{{cite news|title=NCRB 2018 data: Every fourth rape victim in India a minor, 94% victims knew offenders|url=https://www.financialexpress.com/india-news/ncrb-2018-data-every-fourth-rape-victim-in-india-a-minor-94-victims-knew-offenders/1819123/publisher=financialexpress.com|access-date=27 September 2020}}</ref> This high percentage of perpetrators being a close family member (Father/Brother) or acquaintance has remained constant over the years.<ref name="The Hindu">{{cite news|url=http://www.thehindu.com/opinion/lead/good-laws-bad-implementation/article5639799.ece|title=Good laws, bad implementation|newspaper=[[The Hindu]]|date=1 February 2014|access-date=1 February 2014|author=Vasundhara Sirnate|author-link=Vasundhara Sirnate|location=Chennai, India}}</ref>

In 2015, the ''[[The Times of India|Times of India]]'' reported 1300 rapes and 1500 [[Sexual abuse|molestation]] cases were reported in two months from January to February 2015.<ref>{{cite news|title=1300 rapes and 1500 molestation cases reported in just 2 months|url=http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/delhi/300-rapes-and-500-molestation-cases-reported-in-just-2-months/articleshow/46488674.cms|website=The Times of India|date=8 March 2015 |publisher=The Times of India|access-date=3 June 2016}}</ref> But the absolute number of rapes reported have remained broadly similar since 2015.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.aljazeera.com/news/2016/08/india-34000-cases-rape-reported-2015-160831140518208.html|title=India: More than 34,000 cases of rape reported in 2015}}</ref>

As of 2018, [[Madhya Pradesh]] had the highest raw number of rape reports among Indian states.<ref>{{cite news|author=Shaswati Das|title=Women most unsafe in Hindi heartland states, MP registers the highest number of rapes at 15,450|url=https://www.livemint.com/news/india/uttar-pradesh-most-unsafe-for-women-madhya-pradesh-records-maximum-rapes-says-ncrb-2018-data-11578567097964.html|publisher=livemint.com |date=10 January 2020|access-date=20 September 2020}}</ref> By end-2023, however, Madhya Pradesh was 3rd on the list with 2979 cases, while [[Rajasthan]] (5078) and [[Uttar Pradesh]] (3516) reported the most cases of rape. Rajasthan also had the highest rape rate among all states (12.8 per 100,000 women), while the [[Union territory|Union Territory]] of [[Chandigarh]] had the highest rate nationwide (17.9).<ref name=":2" /> Among metropolitan cities, the national capital of [[Delhi]] had the highest incidence of rape, while [[Jaipur]] had the highest rape rate.<ref name=":2" />

In 2016, Union [[Ministry of Women and Child Development|Minister for Women and Child Development]] [[Maneka Gandhi]] reported to the [[Lok Sabha]] that 13,766 cases of child rape were reported to the National Crime Records Bureau in 2014.<ref>{{cite web|title=13,766 cases of child rapes reported in 2014|url=https://www.indiatoday.in/mail-today/story/child-rapes-shoot-up-in-three-years-287094-2015-08-07|website=India Today|date=8 August 2015 |access-date=4 June 2016}}</ref> India ranked 46 in the ranking of reported rape cases per 100,000 population in 2010.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nationmaster.com/country-info/stats/Crime/Rape-rate|title=Countries Compared by Crime > Rape rate. International Statistics at NationMaster.com|website=www.nationmaster.com|access-date=2016-11-23}}</ref>

===Indonesia===
The United Nations Multi-country Study on Men and Violence studied three different sites of Indonesia ([[Jakarta]], rural Java, and [[Jayapura]]). In the rural area, the lifetime prevalence of perpetration of rape towards a female/females was 19.5% and gang rape 7%. When rapists were asked why they perpetrated their last non-partner rape, 76.5% of the men in the three areas averaged cited sexual entitlement, 55.2% entertainment-seeking, and 29.7% anger/punishment.<ref name="unwomen-asiapacific.org"/>

===Italy===
During the first half of the 20th century, in some areas of Italy, rape victims were often expected and forced to marry their rapist. In 1965, a 17-year-old girl from [[Sicily]], created a sensation when&nbsp;– fully supported by her poor family and the local police&nbsp;– she refused to marry the man who [[kidnapping|kidnapped]] and raped her. In refusing this "rehabilitating marriage" to the perpetrator, she went against the traditional social norms of the time,{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}} which dictated a supposed solution, and the rapist was sentenced to ten years in prison followed by two years of internal exile in another region. His seven accomplices were sentenced to five years.{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}} The Criminal Code of Italy also supported this practice, by exonerating the rapist who married the victim.
