The article of law whereby a rapist could extinguish his crime by marrying his victim was abolished in 1981.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.festivaldeldiritto.it/app/document-detail.jsp?id_prodotto=2996&IdC1=1169&css=&tipo=0 |title=Festival del diritto |publisher=Festivaldeldiritto.it |access-date=2013-12-04 |archive-date=16 March 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120316062257/http://www.festivaldeldiritto.it/app/document-detail.jsp?id_prodotto=2996&IdC1=1169&css=&tipo=0 }}</ref> The Franca Viola incident was made into a movie called ''[[La moglie più bella]]''.

In 1999, in an infamous case that gained international attention, the [[Court of Cassation (Italy)|Court of Cassation]] of Italy ordered a new Appeal trial for a man a lower Court had found guilty of the rape of a woman who was wearing tight jeans. The Court did not claim that it is impossible to forcibly remove tight jeans "without the collaboration of the person wearing them" if she resists, but it claimed that such impossibility was plausible only in the given case and that, combined with other more significant evidence come up during the trial, it had led "in abundantiam" to ruling in favour of a new trial.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.neldiritto.it/appgiurisprudenza.asp?id=2281#.X-4KgNhKi-4 |title=CORTE DI CASSAZIONE, SEZ. III PENALE - SENTENZA 5 novembre 2007, n.40542 |website=www.neldiritto.it |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418110538/https://www.neldiritto.it/appgiurisprudenza.asp?id=2281 |archive-date=2021-04-18}}</ref> The court did not equated the removal of the jeans with consent to sexual penetration as stated by Italian and Anglo-Saxon press.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.miolegale.it/massime/jeans-violenza-sessuale/|title=Jeans e violenza sessuale: I pantaloni aderenti non sono una cintura di castità|date=21 July 2008}}</ref> Following this ruling, there was outrage, both in Italy and abroad.{{Citation needed|date=January 2021}} In Italy, female politicians wore jeans to parliament in protest. In 2008, the Court of Cassation did not overturn this infamous ruling:<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.altalex.com/documents/news/2007/06/16/violenza-sessuale-e-jeans-le-precisazioni-della-suprema-corte | title=Violenza sessuale e jeans: Le precisazioni della Suprema Corte | date=4 July 2006 }}</ref> it confirmed the guilty verdict of a lower Court in a case where the victim had removed her own jeans under duress.<ref>{{cite news|last=Swaine |first=Jon |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/italy/2447225/Italy-overturns-ruling-that-women-wearing-tight-jeans-cannot-be-raped.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220112/https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/worldnews/europe/italy/2447225/Italy-overturns-ruling-that-women-wearing-tight-jeans-cannot-be-raped.html |archive-date=12 January 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live |title=Italy overturns ruling that women wearing tight jeans 'cannot be raped' |work=Telegraph |date=23 July 2008 |access-date=2013-12-03 |location=London}}{{cbignore}}</ref>

In another case that sparked outrage, in 2006, the Court of Cassation ruled that a 41-year-old man who raped his 14-year-old stepdaughter could seek to have his sentence reduced&nbsp;– but not overturned&nbsp;– in a new appellate trial, due to the fact that the girl had already been sexually active:<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.eius.it/giurisprudenza/2006/014|title = EIUS - Corte di cassazione, sezione III penale, sentenza 17 febbraio 2006, n. 6329}}</ref> "since the age of 13 [she] had had many sexual relations with men of every age and it's right to assume that at the time of the encounter with the suspect, her personality, from a sexual point of view, was much more developed than what one might normally expect from a girl of her age". Therefore, the Court of Cassation ruled that the first Appeal Court should not have apodictically based its rejection of the existence of mitigating circumstances only on the long-life consequences of the rape.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.altalex.com/documents/news/2006/02/20/lo-stupro-e-meno-grave-se-la-vittima-non-e-piu-vergine-non-lo-dice-la-cassazione | title=Lo stupro è meno grave se la vittima non è piu vergine? Non lo dice la Cassazione | date=21 February 2006 }}</ref>
UNICEF in Italy stated that the decision "seriously violates human rights and the dignity of a minor."<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nbcnews.com/id/wbna11416953 |title=Rape recommendation sparks firestorm |publisher=NBC News |date=17 February 2006 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===Japan===
{{main|Rape in Japan}}

In Japan, rape is defined as a crime of forced sexual intercourse in Article 177 of the [[Penal Code of Japan]]. [[National Police Agency (Japan)|National Police Agency]] publishes rape statistics in Japan.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.npa.go.jp/publications/statistics/sousa/statistics.html |title=犯罪統計 |language=ja |publisher=警察庁 |access-date = 2022-10-20}}</ref>

===Jordan===
Under the law of [[Jordan]], rape is defined by Article 292, which reads: "Whoever has sexual intercourse with a woman, other than his wife, without her consent—whether through coercion, threat, deception, or fraud—is punished with hard labor for no less than 15 years". According to [[UNODC]] statistics, in 2006, the incidence of rapes recorded by the police was 1.9 per 100,000 people.<ref name="unodc1" />

===Latvia===
The laws on sexual offences were modified in [[Latvia]] in 2014, broadening the scope of the legislation. In Latvia, a person who commits an act of sexual intercourse by means of violence, threats, taking advantage of the state of helplessness of the victim, or by abuse of authority, is guilty of rape. (Section 159 of the Criminal Code). Rape and other sexual crimes are defined under ''Chapter XVI'' called "''Criminal Offences against Morals and Sexual Inviolability''". In 2014, Section 48 called ''Aggravating Circumstances'' (which defines circumstances which constitute an aggravation to a crime) was modified, ensuring that marital rape is covered by legislation, by defining as an aggravating circumstance the fact that: "(15) a criminal offence related to violence or threats of violence, or ''against morals and sexual inviolability'', is committed against a person to whom the perpetrator is related in the first or the second degree of kinship, ''against the spouse or former spouse, or against a person with whom the perpetrator is or has been in unregistered marital relationship'', or against a person with whom the perpetrator has a joint (single) household".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://likumi.lv/doc.php?id=88966|title=Krimināllikums|work=Likumi.lv|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref><ref>''Note'': Before this amendment, crimes involving violence and threat of thereof, committed against relatives, spouses/partners, ex-spouses/partners, or other family members, did constitute an aggravating circumstance, but there was no explicit reference to sexual offenses. (while marital rape was not excluded from the definition of rape, according to some sources [from 2005] "''In theory, rape and sexual assault between married partners should be prosecuted and sentenced as non-marital rape or sexual assault would be; in practice, however, the CoE stated that these marital crimes are not brought before Latvian courts (Nov. 2002)''"." [http://www.refworld.org/docid/45f147fd11.html]</ref> In 2008, according to data by UNODC, the incidence of rapes recorded by the police was 4.4 per 100,000 people.<ref name="unodc1" /> In ''J. L. v. Latvia'' (2012),<ref>{{cite web |title=ECHR: J.L. v. Latvia Publication  |url=http://sim.law.uu.nl/SIM/CaseLaw/hof.nsf/d0cd2c2c444d8d94c12567c2002de990/986815722cbac2f4c12579df00443721?OpenDocument |website=SIM |access-date=10 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141020085613/http://sim.law.uu.nl/SIM/CaseLaw/hof.nsf/d0cd2c2c444d8d94c12567c2002de990/986815722cbac2f4c12579df00443721?OpenDocument |archive-date=20 October 2014 |date=13 January 2014}}</ref> the [[European Court of Human Rights]] found that Latvia had failed to comply with its obligation under Article 3 of the [[European Convention on Human Rights]] to carry out an effective investigation into allegations of ill-treatment, because it had failed to properly investigate a prisoner's allegations of rape and assault by fellow inmates, who sought revenge against the victim due to his co-operation with the police.

===Lebanon===
{{Main|Campaign Against Lebanese Rape Law - Article 522}}

In December 2016, the [[Campaign Against Lebanese Rape Law - Article 522]] was launched in order to abolish the article that allowed a rapist to avoid prison by marrying the victim. Prior to its abolishment in February 2017,<ref>D.K. [http://nna-leb.gov.lb/en/show-news/75356/Justice-Parliamentary-Committee-abrogates-Article-522-of-Criminal-Code "Justice Parliamentary Committee abrogates Article 522 of Criminal Code"] National News Agency. Lebanese Ministry of Information 15 February 2017. Accessed 21 February 2017.</ref> the article read: "If a valid contract of marriage is made between the perpetrator of any of the offences mentioned in this section, and the victim, the prosecution is suspended. If judgment was already passed, the implementation of the punishment is suspended."<ref>Equality Now [http://www.equalitynow.org/sites/default/files/B+20_Report_EN.pdf] "Ending Sex Discrimination in the Law" Equality Now, January 2015, Accessed 19 February 2017. Original; [http://www.ilo.org/dyn/natlex/docs/ELECTRONIC/89873/103350/F300391946/LBN89873%20Arab.pdf]</ref>
Since February 2017, other articles of the penal code are being amended to reinforce penalties against rapists that commit sexual assault on girls under 15.<ref>Merhi, Nada [https://www.lorientlejour.com/article/1035651/projet-dabrogation-de-larticle-522-reactions-mitigees-de-la-societe-civile.html "Projet d'abrogation de l'article 522 : réactions mitigées de la société civile"] L'Orient-Le Jour 17 February 2017. Accessed 3 March 2017.</ref>

===Lesotho===
Rape is one of [[Lesotho]]'s main social issues. According to [[UNODC]], the incidence of rapes recorded in 2008 by the police in Lesotho was the highest incidence of any country.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite web|url=http://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/Crime-statistics/Sexual_violence_sv_against_children_and_rape.xls |title=Crime Statistics: Sexual Violence Against Children and Rape |publisher=Unodc.org |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref> In a study of 1,049 women, 33% said they had been raped by the age of 18. In 66% of cases the rapist was a boyfriend.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://apha.confex.com/apha/133am/techprogram/paper_114115.htm |title=Magnitude of sexual violence in Lesotho |publisher=Apha.confex.com |date=12 December 2005 |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=29 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029201559/https://apha.confex.com/apha/133am/techprogram/paper_114115.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> In the 2009 [[Demographic and Health Surveys|DHS survey]] 15.7% of men said that a husband is justified in hitting or beating his wife if she refuses to have sex with him, while 16% said a husband is justified to use force to have sex.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.measuredhs.com/pubs/pdf/FR241/FR241%5BNEW_completeHHQst_3March2012%5D.pdf |title=Lesotho: Demographic and Health Survey 2009 |publisher=Measuredhs.com |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref> HIV/AIDS in Lesotho is a very serious problem, with 23.1% of adults aged 15 to 49 living with it.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.unaids.org/en/regionscountries/countries/lesotho/ |title=Lesotho |publisher=Unaids.org |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> In a study, researchers have concluded that "Given the high prevalence of HIV in Lesotho, programs should address women's right to control their sexuality."<ref>{{cite journal|title= Sexual violence in Lesotho|date=12 August 2013 |pmid=17209284 | volume=37 |issue=4 |journal=Stud Fam Plann |pages=269–80 | last1 = Brown | first1 = L | last2 = Thurman | first2 = T | last3 = Bloem | first3 = J | last4 = Kendall | first4 = C|doi=10.1111/j.1728-4465.2006.00105.x }}</ref>

===Libya===
Victims of rape in [[Libya]] are often deemed as having 'dishonoured' their families and communities, and may face serious violence, including honour killings. According to [[UNHCR]], "In Libya when rape occurs, it seems to be a whole village or town which is seen to be dishonoured".<ref name="bbc.co.uk">{{cite news| url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-africa-13760895 |work=BBC News |title=Libya rape victims 'face honour killings'}}</ref> Women who have been raped experience extreme shame; according to a charity worker, being raped is "worse than death for them [the victims]".<ref name="bbc.co.uk"/>

===Mexico===
[[Mexico]] has a federal law, as well as state laws. Mexican laws have been modernized significantly from the 1990s onwards. Rape laws used to include stipulations that the penalty was to be reduced if the victim had "provoked" the attacker.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.latinamericanstudies.org/mexico/rape.htm |title=Mexican lawmakers review rape law |publisher=Latinamericanstudies.org |date=19 September 2001 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> In 2005, the [[Supreme Court of Mexico]] ruled that forced sex in marriage is rape.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.un.org/spanish/News/story.asp?NewsID=5773#.UjNZlX9edO4 |title=Centro de Noticias de la ONU - México: UNIFEM aplaude tipificación como delito de violación dentro del matrimonio |publisher=Un.org |access-date=2013-12-03|date=17 November 2005 }}</ref> In doing so, it overturned its prior verdict from 1994 when it had ruled that the laws on rape were inapplicable in marriage.<ref name="nytimes.com">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2005/11/17/international/americas/17mexico.html?_r=0|title=Mexican Court Says Sex Attack by a Husband Is Still a Rape|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|access-date=2013-12-04|first1=Elisabeth|last1=Malkin|first2=Ginger|last2=Thompson|date=17 November 2005}}</ref> In Mexico, the rape laws did not include a statutory exemption for marriage, but were, as elsewhere, generally understood as inapplicable in this context. This has started to be challenged in the late 20th century. Following the Court's decision in 1994, women's organizations worked to pass state laws against marital rape in order to overturn this precedent. The new 2005 verdict has been interpreted as evidence of the improvement of the position of women in the country.<ref name="nytimes.com"/> Mexico has recently been plagued by scandals of [[child sexual abuse]] in [[Catholic]] institutions.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5jHFt_Rut8_u89I1UBLUuadghpzPw?hl=en |title=AFP: Mexico Catholic Church seeks child sex abuse pardon |work=Google News |date=13 April 2010 |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140130145034/https://www.google.com/hostednews/afp/article/ALeqM5jHFt_Rut8_u89I1UBLUuadghpzPw?hl=en |archive-date=30 January 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ipsnews.net/2013/07/activists-demand-justice-for-victims-of-clerical-sex-abuse-in-mexico/ |title=Activists Demand Justice for Victims of Clerical Sex Abuse in Mexico - Inter Press Service |date=25 July 2013 |publisher=Ipsnews.net |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> A 2013 violent [[gang rape]] of six [[Spain|Spanish]] tourist women in [[Acapulco]] has raised questions about how safe Mexico is for tourists.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-latin-america-21350187 |title=Mexico hunts Acapulco Spanish tourist rape gang |work=BBC News |date=6 February 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

===Netherlands===
The law on rape in the [[Netherlands]] states that: "A person who by an act of violence or another act or by threat of violence or threat of another act compels a person to submit to acts comprising or including sexual penetration of the body is guilty of rape and liable to a term of imprisonment of not more than twelve years or a fine of the fifth category."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.wetboek-online.nl/wet/Wetboek%20van%20Strafrecht.html#1824 |title=Wetboek van Strafrecht |publisher=Wetboek-online.nl |access-date=2014-02-03}}</ref>

Apart from the offence of 'rape', there are also other sexual offences. Marital rape was made illegal in 1991; before that date, rape was defined as a man forcing, by violence or threat of thereof, a woman to engage in sexual intercourse outside of marriage.<ref>http://www.bjutijdschriften.nl/tijdschrift/rem/2012/1/ReM_2212-2508_2012_002_001_005.pdf {{dead link|date=April 2015}}</ref>

According to a 2014 study published by the [[European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights]], the Netherlands had the fourth highest prevalence rate of physical and sexual violence against women in Europe, with 45% of women having experienced such violence, which is well above the European average of 33%.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iamexpat.nl/read-and-discuss/expat-page/news/dutch-women-assaulted-per-cent-statistics|title=45 per cent of Dutch women have been assaulted|last=Wedia |date=7 March 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://fra.europa.eu/sites/default/files/fra-2014-vaw-survey-main-results_en.pdf |title=Violence against women: an EU-wide survey |access-date=2014-05-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140307224554/http://fra.europa.eu/sites/default/files/fra-2014-vaw-survey-main-results_en.pdf |archive-date=7 March 2014 }}</ref>

In 2020 an investigation by the daily newspaper [[Algemeen Dagblad]] revealed that since 2017 a judge has never imposed the maximum prison sentence of 12 years in a Dutch rape case. The highest sentence was six years, the lowest 21 days. On average, a rapist was jailed for a year and five months.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ad.nl/binnenland/zelden-rechtszaak-na-verkrachting~a7b27ec1/ |title=Zelden rechtszaak na verkrachting |access-date=2020-10-14 }}</ref>

===Nicaragua===
In a 2010 report on sexual violence in [[Nicaragua]], Amnesty International stated that "Rape of girls is endemic". In Nicaragua, between 1998 and 2008, police recorded 14,377 cases of rape, with more than two thirds of reports involving girls under the age of 17. Reporting of rape, however, is estimated to be low, because rape victims often face social hostility and indifference from authorities.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/amr43/008/2010/en/ |title=listen to their voices and act |date=25 November 2010 |access-date=2016-12-04 }}</ref> Since 2008, abortion is illegal without any exception, and this ban has been criticized as oppressive to rape victims who become pregnant.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/search/?contentType=2561|title=Turkmenistan|work=Amnesty.org|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref>

In 2012, Nicaragua enacted Law no 779&nbsp;– Integral Law against Violence against Women (''Ley Integral contra la Violencia hacia la Mujer''). This law criminalizes a wide range of acts of violence against women, such as domestic violence, including marital rape.<ref>{{cite web |title=Ley No. 779 |url=http://legislacion.asamblea.gob.ni/SILEG/Iniciativas.nsf/0/8f45bac34395458c062578320075bde4/$FILE/Ley%20No.%20779%20Ley%20Integral%20contra%20la%20Violencia.pdf |publisher=El Presidente de la República de Nicaragua |access-date=10 October 2018}}</ref>

===Nigeria===
According to Amnesty International, police forces in [[Nigeria]] are reported to have perpetrated acts of rape and other sexual abuse against women, in public locations, or while women were transferred to police stations, or while women visited male detainees in police custody; and sometimes police used sexual violence in order to extract confessions and other information.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr44/005/2014/en/ |access-date=22 May 2014 |title=Torture in Nigeria: In summary |date=13 May 2014 }}</ref>

A study of students of the Polytechnic, [[Ibadan]] found that in their lifetimes 1.7% (2.5% of males and 1.1% of females) had raped and 2.7% (5.3% of males and 0.9% of females) had attempted rape.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ajol.info/index.php/ajrh/article/viewFile/83689/73709 |title=Prevalence and Factors Associated with Perpetration on Non-Consensual Sex among Students of a Tertiary Institution in Ibadan, Nigeria |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref>

Out of a sample of 295 female students from [[Ebonyi State University Abakaliki]] in Southeast Nigeria, 36.7% had experienced sexual harassment/victimization at least once on campus. Of this, 32.4% had been raped (10.8% of the sample).<ref>{{Cite journal|url=http://www.ajol.info/index.php/jcmphc/article/view/84665 |title=Prevalence of sexual harassment/victimization of female students in Ebonyi State University Abakaliki, southeast Nigeria &#124; Ogbonnaya &#124; Journal of Community Medicine and Primary Health Care |journal=Journal of Community Medicine and Primary Health Care |volume=23 |issue=1–2 |pages=55–67 |date=21 January 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03|last1=Emma-Echiegu |first1=N. B. |last2=Ogbonnaya |first2=C. E. |last3=Ogbonnaya |first3=L. U. }}</ref>

A study comparing the sexual practises of 12- to 19-year-old students with and without mild/moderate intellectual disabilities from schools across [[Oyo State]], Nigeria found that 68.3% of the sexually experienced intellectually disabled females reported a history of rape victimization compared to 2.9% of the sexually experienced non-disabled females.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Differences in HIV knowledge and sexual practices of learners with intellectual disabilities and non-disabled learners in Nigeria |pmc=3568677 | pmid=23394898 |volume=16 |year=2013 |journal=J Int AIDS Soc |article-number=17331 | last1 = Aderemi | first1 = TJ | last2 = Pillay | first2 = BJ | last3 = Esterhuizen | first3 = TM |issue=1 | doi=10.7448/ias.16.1.17331}}</ref>

A study analysing the hospital records of 76 sexual assault victims in [[Ile-Ife]] from 2007 to 2011 found that the majority (76.1%) of the victims that sought help at a hospital did so within 24 hours of their sexual assault, but forensic evidence was not gathered because [[rape kits]] have yet to be introduced in the country.<ref name="Badejoko_Nigeria">{{cite journal|last1=Badejoko|first1=Olusegun|last2=Anyabolu|first2=Henry|last3=Badejoko|first3=Bolaji|last4=Ijarotimi|first4=Adebimpe|last5=Kuti|first5=Oluwafemi|last6=Adejuyigbe|first6=Ebunoluwa|title=Sexual assault in Ile-Ife, Nigeria|journal=Nigerian Medical Journal|date=2014|volume=55|issue=3|pages=254–259|doi=10.4103/0300-1652.132065|pmid=25013260|pmc=4089057 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

In a 2013 poll of 585 randomly selected adults from six Nigerian geopolitical zones by NOI Polls, 34% answered "What do you think is the most prevalent cause of rape in the society?" with 'indecent dressing'. 29% said they personally knew a victim of rape.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://noi-polls.com/index.php?s_id=3&p_id=220&p_pt=1&parent=11#.Umw8R_mTh-d |title=Welcome to NOI-Polls |publisher=Noi-polls.com |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-date=29 October 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131029204752/http://noi-polls.com/index.php?s_id=3&p_id=220&p_pt=1&parent=11#.Umw8R_mTh-d }}</ref>

===North Korea===
The situation regarding sexual violence in [[North Korea]] is very difficult to assess because of the unwillingness of the North Korean authorities to allow foreign investigators access in the country. According to Amnesty International, the analysis of satellite images of political prison camps ([[kwanliso]]) suggest that these camps are in continuous use and expansion. Amnesty International stated that hundreds of thousands of people, including children, are detained in these institutions, where they are subjected to extreme forms of abuse and violence, including rape. The organization cited a former security official at a kwanliso who worked there in the 1980s until the mid-1990s, and who confirmed these accounts.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/asa24/010/2013/en/ |date=2013 |access-date=22 May 2014 |title=North Korea: New satellite images show continued investment in the infrastructure of repression }}</ref> A United Nations panel has stated that the inmate population at political camps has been subjected to systematic extermination, torture, rape, forced abortions and starvation.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-26223180|title=UN North Korea report main findings|journal=BBC News|date=17 February 2014|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref> According to the UN report, women at these camps are systematically subjected to rape by guards or bought and sold by human traffickers in China.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.euronews.com/2014/02/17/north-korea-s-gulag-horrors-condemned-by-un|title=North Korea's gulag horrors condemned by UN|date=17 February 2014|work=EuroNews.com|access-date=18 March 2017|archive-date=5 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170805025813/http://www.euronews.com/2014/02/17/north-korea-s-gulag-horrors-condemned-by-un}}</ref>

===Norway===
Rape is defined by Section 192 of the Criminal Code which states:<ref name="ub.uio.no">{{cite web |title=The General Civil Penal Code |url=http://app.uio.no/ub/ujur/oversatte-lover/data/lov-19020522-010-eng.pdf |website=UIO |publisher=Ministry of Justice and the Police |access-date=10 October 2018}}</ref> "Any person who a) engages in sexual activity by means of violence or threats, or b) engages in sexual activity with any person who is unconscious or incapable for any other reason of resisting the act, or c) by means of violence or threats compels any person to engage in sexual activity with another person, or to carry out similar acts with himself or herself, shall be guilty of rape [...]." Sexual crimes in Norway are defined in Chapter 19&nbsp;– ''Sexual Offenses'', which contains Sections 192 to 208.<ref name="ub.uio.no"/>

The incidence of reported rape in [[Norway]] for 2010 is given as about 35 out of 100,000; there is no in-depth national statistic.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.politi.no/vedlegg/lokale_vedlegg/oslo/Vedlegg_1309.pdf |title=Voldtekt i den Globale Byen |publisher=Oslo Politiditrikt |date=May 2011 |access-date=2013-02-03 |language=no |archive-date=10 June 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170610163534/https://www.politi.no/vedlegg/lokale_vedlegg/oslo/Vedlegg_1309.pdf }}</ref> A report released in February 2014, found that 9.4 percent of the 2435 women surveyed and 1.1 percent of the 2091 interviewed men stated that they were raped.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.regjeringen.no/pages/38635924/NKVTS_vold-voldtekt-2014.pdf |title=Vold og voldtekt i Norge |publisher=Nasjonalt kunnskapssenter om vold og traumatisk stress | date=February 2014 |access-date=17 May 2014 |language=no |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140518204926/http://www.regjeringen.no/pages/38635924/NKVTS_vold-voldtekt-2014.pdf |archive-date=18 May 2014}}</ref> A new report released in February 2023, found that 22 percent of the women surveyed stated that they were raped.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.vg.no/nyheter/innenriks/i/abKO1d/ny-rapport-en-av-fem-norske-kvinner-har-blitt-voldtatt |title=Ny rapport: Én av fem norske kvinner har blitt voldtatt
 |publisher=VG | date=February 2023 |access-date=28 February 2023 |language=no }}</ref>

====Legislative history====
Norway overhauled its sexual offences legislation in 2000. The definition of rape was broadened to include also acts committed with persons incapable of resisting, rather than only acts enforced through direct violence or threat.<ref name="amnesty.dk1">{{cite web |url=http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |title=Case closed: rape and human rights in the Nordic countries |website=www.amnesty.dk |access-date=15 January 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110317185917/http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |archive-date=17 March 2011 }}</ref> The law is gender-neutral. In 1974, the [[Supreme Court of Norway]] confirmed the applicability of the rape law to marital intercourse, convicting for the first time a man of raping his wife.<ref name="amnesty.dk1"/>

====Concerns====
There are concerns in Norway about the low reporting and conviction rate for rape. According to Amnesty International, 84% of rape cases reported to the police do not reach court; of those that reach trial, 36% end in acquittal.<ref name="amnesty.dk1"/> In 2003, the [[CEDAW]] Committee expressed concern about the situation of sexual violence in Norway, stating, "[The Committee] is also concerned that an extremely low percentage of reported rapes results in convictions and that the police and public prosecutors dismiss an increasing number of such cases."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www1.umn.edu/humanrts/cedaw/cedaw-norway2003.html|title=University of Minnesota Human Rights Library|work=UMN.edu|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref>

===Pakistan===
{{Main|Rape in Pakistan}}

Rape in Pakistan has been notable, and in recent times have continued to spike. In one case, a teenage girl was burnt alive, as she resisted the rape.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/pakistan/Pakistani-girl-burnt-alive-for-resisting-rape/articleshow/21306571.cms |title=Pakistani girl burnt alive for resisting rape - The Times of India |publisher=Timesofindia.IndiaTimes.com |access-date=3 December 2013}}</ref>

In another notable case a woman was raped on the orders of a [[Union councils of Pakistan|village council]], which functions as a lower-level judiciary. In 2002, 30-year-old [[Mukhtaran Bibi]] was gang-raped on the orders of the village council as an "honor rape" after allegations that her 12-year-old brother had had sexual relations with a woman from a higher caste.<ref name="Greenberg" /> Although custom would expect her to commit suicide after being raped,<ref name="NYTimes Kristof 2004-09-29" /><ref name="NYTimes Masood 2009-03-09" /><ref name="UN 2006-05-06" /> Mukhtaran spoke up, and pursued the case, which was picked up by both domestic and international media. On 1 September 2002, an [[Anti Terrorism Court of Pakistan|anti-terrorism court]] sentenced six men (including the four rapists) to death for rape. In 2005, the [[Lahore High Court]] cited "insufficient evidence" and acquitted 5 of the 6 convicted, and commuted the punishment for the sixth man to a [[life sentence]]. Mukhtaran and the government appealed this decision, and the [[Supreme Court of Pakistan|Supreme Court]] suspended the acquittal and held appeal hearings.<ref name="BBC 2005-06-28" /> In 2011, the Supreme Court too acquitted the accused.

In 2015, a massive child molesting crime in Pakistani history was discovered. About 280 were raped and filmed. Some of these rapists used these video clips to blackmail the parents of those children. Most of victims were below 14 years old.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.dw.com/en/massive-child-abuse-scandal-unveiled-in-pakistan/a-18636820|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150811190901/http://www.dw.com/en/massive-child-abuse-scandal-unveiled-in-pakistan/a-18636820|url-status=live|title=Massive child abuse scandal unveiled in Pakistan|first=Manasi|last=Gopalakrishnan|date=9 August 2015|archive-date=11 August 2015|work=Deutsche Welle (www.dw.com)|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref> Malik Ahmed Saeed Khan, a member of Provincial Assembly (MPA) of Punjab, also a member of the ruling party, [[Pakistan Muslim League (N)|Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz]], was accused for his involvement in this series of crimes,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://dailythepatriot.com/kasur-child-abuse-scandal-role-of-mpa-malik-ahmad-saeed-khan/|title=Kasur Child Abuse scandal: Role of MPA Malik Ahmad Saeed Khan|date=8 August 2015|access-date=22 August 2015|archive-date=10 August 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150810210715/http://dailythepatriot.com/kasur-child-abuse-scandal-role-of-mpa-malik-ahmad-saeed-khan/|url-status=dead}}</ref> including selling rape video clips (around 400 clips) to the international market.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.voice.pk/videos/kasur-child-abuse-scandal-pmln-mpa-malik-saeed-supplied-these-videos-to-international-market/|title=Kasur Child Abuse Scandal: PMLN MPA Malik Saeed Supplied These Videos to International Market - Voice.pk|first=Ahsan|last=Mukhtar|date=8 August 2015|work=Voice.pk|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref>

===Papua New Guinea===
{{Main|Sexual violence in Papua New Guinea}}

[[Papua New Guinea]] has a very high rate of sexual [[violence]], which has been attributed to the interaction between a very male-dominated culture and a culture which is also very accepting of violence in day-to-day life.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2013/09/130914-rape-asia-pacific-un-men-violence-women/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130916011153/http://news.nationalgeographic.com/news/2013/09/130914-rape-asia-pacific-un-men-violence-women/ |archive-date=16 September 2013 |title=UN Study Looks at High Rate of Rape |publisher=News.nationalgeographic.com |date=14 September 2013 |access-date=3 December 2013}}</ref> Marital rape was criminalized in 2003.<ref name="unwomen-asiapacific.org"/> According to a 1993 survey by the PNG Institute of Medical Research, an estimated 55% of Papua New Guinean women have experienced rape.<ref>{{cite web |title= Key Statistics |url= http://www.rugbyleagueagainstviolence.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/Key-Statistics.pdf |access-date= 12 November 2014 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20141112095030/http://www.rugbyleagueagainstviolence.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/06/Key-Statistics.pdf |archive-date= 12 November 2014}}</ref>

The United Nations Multi-country Study on Men and Violence found that 62% of men from [[Bougainville Island]] had raped a woman and 7.6% had raped a man. 14% had participated in gang rape. 7% said they had been raped by another man.

Non-partner rape was more commonly perpetrated than partner rape. 69.3% of the men who reported rape had raped more than once. 15.5% had raped four or more women or girls. 71% reported their motivation behind rape being sexual entitlement, 63% said they raped for entertainment, and 50% said they raped out of anger or to punish a woman. 52.2% had been jailed for their crime. Out of the nine areas surveyed, this was the highest rate of imprisonment.<ref name="unwomen-asiapacific.org"/>

===Qatar===
In [[Qatar]], like in most countries in the Middle East, sex outside of marriage is illegal. Women who report rape or sexual violence risk being charged with "illicit relations".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/news/qatar-un-review-crucial-reforms-needed-protect-women-and-migrant-workers-2014-05-07|title=Qatar UN review: Crucial reforms needed to protect women and migrant workers|work=Amnesty.org|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref> Amnesty International has reported that migrant [[domestic workers]] are at very high risk of sexual abuse.<ref>{{cite web |title=MY SLEEP IS MY BREAK |date=23 April 2014 |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/mde22/004/2014/en/ |access-date=22 May 2014 }}</ref> In 2012, the [[UN Committee against Torture]] made reference to "numerous allegations by migrant workers of physical abuse, sexual violence, rape and attempted rape".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bettercarenetwork.org/violence/search/closeup.asp?infoID=28271|title=Welcome to the Better Care Network! - Better Care Network|work=BetterCareNetwork.org|access-date=18 March 2017|archive-date=23 September 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923184051/http://www.bettercarenetwork.org/violence/search/closeup.asp?infoID=28271}}</ref>

===Rwanda===
{{Further|Rape during the Rwandan genocide}}
The UN estimates that in [[Rwanda]] between 100,000 and 250,000 women were [[Rape during the Rwandan genocide|raped during the Rwandan genocide]] in 1994.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.un.org/en/preventgenocide/rwanda/about/bgsexualviolence.shtml |title=Background Information on Sexual Violence used as a Tool of War - Outreach Programme on the Rwanda Genocide and the United Nations |publisher=Un.org |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Rape was used as a weapon of war, and there are numerous children who were born from these rapes.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/newsnight/8768943.stm |title=Newsnight - Rwanda's children of rape |work=BBC News |date=30 June 2010 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Many of the women who were raped were also infected with [[HIV/AIDS]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/programmes/panorama/3586409.stm |title=Programmes &#124; Panorama &#124; Rwanda: 10 quick facts |work=BBC News |date=2 April 2004 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

In 2009 Rwanda adopted a law (''Law on prevention and punishment of Gender Based Violence'') which recognizes, for the first time in the country's history, marital rape as a crime.<ref>{{cite web |title=Rwanda: Law No. 59/2008 of 2008 on Prevention and Punishment of Gender-Based Violence |url=http://www.refworld.org/docid/4a3f88812.html |website=Refworld |publisher=United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees |access-date=4 June 2018 |language=en |date=10 September 2008}}</ref>

=== Saudi Arabia ===
Saudi Arabia has general crime rates 100 times lower than that of America. In 1981, the rates of forcible rape were 0.33 out of 100,000. Badr-el-din Ali suggests this may be due to Saudi Arabia having a [[synnomic]] state of culture, where everyone uncompromisingly shares the same values.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=ALI|first=BADR-EL-DIN|date=1985-01-01|title=Islamic Law And Crime: The Case Of Saudi Arabia|journal=International Journal of Comparative and Applied Criminal Justice|volume=9|issue=1–2|pages=45–57|doi=10.1080/01924036.1985.9688820|issn=0192-4036}}</ref>

===Somalia===
In 2012, the reported nationwide prevalence rate ranged from 2% to 13%.<ref name="Shdrt">{{cite web|title=Somalia Human Development Report 2012|url=http://hdr.undp.org/sites/default/files/reports/242/somalia_report_2012.pdf|publisher=UNDP|access-date=20 February 2014}}</ref> Most incidents of sexual assault occurred within the context of the insurgency in southern Somalia. Over the first quarter of 2013, Amnesty International reported that 56.7% of victims in Mogadishu were internally displaced persons. According to the UN, there were at least 2,924 rape cases in IDP settlements in 2012. A third of the victims were under the age of 18. 70% of the perpetrators were armed men wearing uniforms, although it was not always clear whether they were members of militias, security forces or other individuals or groups.<ref>{{cite web|title=Rape and sexual violence in Somalia - An ongoing epidemic |date=30 August 2013 |url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr52/009/2013/en/ |publisher=Amnesty International |access-date=25 June 2014 }}</ref> To address the issue, the central authorities as of December 2013 were in the process of forming a special crime unit to investigate and counter gender-based violence, as well as constructing a clinic set aside for victims of sexual assault. The national judiciary, security and police forces were all concurrently receiving specialized gender training as part of the broader reform effort.<ref name="Sphaswffftrotmv">{{cite news|title=Somalia President Hassan applauds Somali women for fighting for the rights of the most vulnerable|url=http://horseedmedia.net/2013/12/04/somalia-president-hassan-applauds-somali-women-fighting-rights-vulnerable/|access-date=20 February 2014|newspaper=Horseed Media|date=4 December 2013}}</ref> In June 2014, the Somali government also launched a National Action Plan against sexual violence in conjunction with local civil society groups.<ref name="Prsgwulogs">{{cite news|title=Press Release: Somali Government welcomes UK's leadership on Global Summit to End Sexual Violence in Conflict and given particular attention to Somalia |url=http://goobjoog.com/en/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=2704:press-release-somali-government-welcomes-uk-s-leadership-on-global-summit-to-end-sexual-violence-in-conflict-and-given-particular-attention-to-somalia&catid=124:local-news&Itemid=653 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20140622195116/http://goobjoog.com/en/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=2704:press-release-somali-government-welcomes-uk-s-leadership-on-global-summit-to-end-sexual-violence-in-conflict-and-given-particular-attention-to-somalia&catid=124:local-news&Itemid=653 |archive-date=22 June 2014 |access-date=22 June 2014 |agency=Goobjoog |date=10 June 2014}}</ref>

===South Africa===
{{Main|Sexual violence in South Africa}}

The [[Criminal Law (Sexual Offences and Related Matters) Amendment Act, 2007]] is the relevant legislation in [[South Africa]]. Despite the fact that this act provides modern and progressive laws, that ban rape and other forms of sexual abuse, including sexual violence within marriage, South Africa remains a country where sexual attacks are common. The country has some of the highest incidences of [[Child sexual abuse|child and baby rape]] in the world with more than 67,000 cases of rape and sexual assaults against children reported in 2000, with welfare groups believing that unreported incidents could be up to 10 times higher.<ref name="time"/> In 2001, a nine-month-old was raped and likely lost consciousness as the pain was too much to bear.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://abcnews.go.com/WNT/story?id=130199&page=1|title=Baby rape sparks outrage|publisher=abcnews.com|date=30 July 2002|access-date=2011-07-12}}</ref> Another nine-month-old baby was raped by six men, aged between 24 and 66, after the infant had been left unattended by her teenage mother. A four-year-old girl died after being raped by her father. A 14-month-old girl was raped by her two uncles. In February 2002, an eight-month-old infant was reportedly gang raped by four men. One has been charged. The infant has required extensive reconstructive surgery. The eight-month-old infant's injuries were so extensive, increased attention on prosecution has occurred.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/444213 |title=Child rape in South Africa |website=Medscape |access-date=2010-12-31 |archive-date=29 December 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101229174131/http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/444213 }}</ref> A significant contributing factor for the escalation in child abuse is the widespread myth in [[HIV]]-ravaged South Africa that having sex with a virgin will cure a man of [[AIDS]].<ref name=telegraph>{{cite news|last=Flanagan |first=Jane |url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=/news/2001/11/11/wrape11.xml|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20031002162453/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/main.jhtml?xml=/news/2001/11/11/wrape11.xml|archive-date=2 October 2003|title=South African men rape babies as 'cure' for Aids |work=The Daily Telegraph |location=UK |date=11 November 2001|access-date=15 May 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.mediaaids.org/content/page/having_sex_with_a_virgin_will_cure_hiv |title=Having Sex With a Virgin Will Cure HIV |publisher=mediaaids.org |access-date=28 May 2015}}</ref> According to official figures, circa 11% of South Africans are infected with the virus.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.avert.org/safricastats.htm |title=South Africa HIV & AIDS Statistics |publisher=[[AVERT]].org |access-date=11 December 2011|date=21 July 2015 }}</ref> Edith Kriel, a social worker who helps child victims in the [[Eastern Cape]], said: "Child abusers are often relatives of their victims&nbsp;– even their fathers and providers."<ref name="telegraph"/>

One in three of the 4,000 women questioned by the Community of Information, Empowerment and Transparency said they had been raped in the past year.<ref name="bbc1">{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/258446.stm |title=South Africa's rape shock|work=BBC News |date=19 January 1999 |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref> More than 25% of South African men questioned in a survey admitted to raping someone; of those, nearly half said they had raped more than one person, according to a new study conducted by the Medical Research Council (MRC).<ref>"[http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/8107039.stm South African rape survey shock]." BBC News. 18 June 2009.</ref><ref>"[https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/jun/17/south-africa-rape-survey Quarter of men in South Africa admit rape, survey finds]"</ref> A 2010 study led by the government-funded Medical Research Foundation says that in Gauteng province, more than 37 percent of men said they had raped a woman. Nearly 7 percent of the 487 men surveyed said they had participated in a gang rape.<ref>[http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2010/11/27/south-africa-rape-study-m_n_788722.html "South Africa Rape Study_ More Than 1 In 3 Men Admit To Rape"]</ref> Among children, a survey found 11% of boys and 4% of girls admitted to forcing someone else to have sex with them while in another survey among 1,500 schoolchildren in the [[Soweto]] [[township]], a quarter of all the boys interviewed said that 'jackrolling', a term for [[gang rape]], was fun.<ref name=time/><ref name=bbc1/>

In 2013 a study of 1991 grade nine boys at 46 secondary schools in Cape Town and Port Elizabeth found that 17.2% had raped.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1136/sextrans-2013-051184.0840 |title=P3.387 Prevalence and Predictors of Rape Perpetration Among Male Secondary School Students in Peri-Urban Xhosa Communities in South Africa |journal=Sexually Transmitted Infections |volume=89 |pages=A270.2–A270 |year=2013 |last1=Kaufman |first1=Z. A. |last2=Kaufman |first2=E. B. |last3=Dringus |first3=S. |last4=Weiss |first4=H. A. |last5=Delany-Moretlwe |first5=S. |last6=Ross |first6=D. A. |doi-access=free }}</ref>

South Africa has some of the highest incidences of child and baby rape in the world.<ref name=time>{{cite news|title=Oprah scandal rocks South Africa |author=Alex Perry|url=http://www.time.com/time/world/article/0,8599,1680715,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071106153917/http://www.time.com/time/world/article/0,8599,1680715,00.html |archive-date=6 November 2007 |newspaper=[[Time (magazine)|Time]] |date=5 November 2007 |access-date=11 December 2011}}</ref> More than 25% of a sample of 1,738 South African men from the [[KwaZulu-Natal]] and [[Eastern Cape]] Provinces admitted when anonymously questioned to raping someone; of those, nearly half said they had raped more than one person, according to a non-peer-reviewed policy brief issued by the Medical Research Council (MRC). 4.95% had raped or attempted rape in the past year at the time of the survey.<ref>{{cite report |title=Understanding Men's Health and Use of Violence: Interface of Rape and HIV in South Africa |url=http://www.mrc.ac.za/gender/violence_hiv.pdf |author-link=Rachel Jewkes |last=Jewkes |first=Rachel |first2=Yandisa |last2=Sikweyiya |first3=Robert |last3=Morrell |first4=Kristin |last4=Dunkle |year=2009 |publisher=[[South African Medical Research Council]] |access-date=24 October 2010 |archive-date=16 May 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110516150322/http://www.mrc.ac.za/gender/violence_hiv.pdf }}</ref> Several news publications extrapolated these results to the rest of the South African population.<ref>{{cite news|title=South African rape survey shock |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/8107039.stm |work=BBC News|date=18 June 2009 |access-date=11 December 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Quarter of men in South Africa admit rape, survey finds |author=David Smith |url=https://www.theguardian.com/world/2009/jun/17/south-africa-rape-survey|newspaper=Guardian |date=17 June 2009 |access-date=11 December 2011 |location=London}}</ref><ref name="irin">{{cite news |title=SOUTH AFRICA: One in four men rape |url=http://www.irinnews.org/report/84909/south-africa-one-in-four-men-rape |newspaper=[[The New Humanitarian|IRIN]] Africa |date=18 June 2009|access-date=11 December 2011}}</ref> The humanitarian news organization [[The New Humanitarian|IRIN]] claims that an estimated 500,000 rapes are committed annually in South Africa.<ref name="irin"/>
[[File:Listening to girls in Zambia (8220719638).jpg|thumb|upright=1.2|In a recent survey of schoolgirls in [[Lusaka]], [[Zambia]], 53% reported that girls in their school have experienced sexual harassment.]]
According to [[University of Durban-Westville]] anthropology lecturer and researcher Suzanne Leclerc-Madlala, the myth that sex with a virgin is a cure for AIDS is not confined to South Africa. "Fellow AIDS researchers in [[Zambia]], [[Zimbabwe]] and [[Nigeria]] have told me that the myth also exists in these countries and that it is being blamed for the high rate of [[Child sexual abuse|sexual abuse against young children]]."<ref>{{cite news|title=Child rape: A taboo within the AIDS taboo |author=Prega Govender |url=http://www.aegis.com/news/suntimes/1999/ST990401.html |newspaper=[[The Sunday Times (South Africa)|The Sunday Times]] |date=4 April 1999 |access-date=11 December 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111209203938/http://www.aegis.com/news/suntimes/1999/ST990401.html |archive-date=9 December 2011}}</ref>

"In South Africa, rape is so common it barely makes the news. The rapes of elderly women and babies are outlined in four-line stories on the inside pages of local newspapers, but most sexual assaults get no public attention."<ref name=star>{{cite news| url=https://www.thestar.com/news/world/2013/02/11/south_africa_gang_rape_a_symbol_of_nations_problem.html
| title=South Africa gang rape a symbol of nation's problem| first=Erin| last=Conway-Smith| date=11 February 2013| access-date=12 March 2013| newspaper=GlobalPost| publisher=Toronto Star Newspapers Ltd}}</ref>

In 2016, the police recorded 39,828 rapes which means rape rate of 71.3.<ref name="South Africa">{{cite web |title=Crime situation in South Africa 1 April 2016 – 31 March 2017 |url=https://www.saps.gov.za/services/final_crime_stats_presentation_24_october_2017.pdf |publisher=South African Police Service |access-date=10 October 2018 |archive-date=28 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171028112642/https://www.saps.gov.za/services/final_crime_stats_presentation_24_october_2017.pdf |url-status=dead }}{{full citation needed|date=October 2018}}</ref>

===South Sudan===
In [[South Sudan]], marital rape is not criminalized; the law on rape excludes it from its definition by stating that "Sexual intercourse by a married couple is not rape, within the meaning of this section". (Art 247).<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.goss-online.org/magnoliaPublic/en/Laws--Legislation--Policies/mainColumnParagraphs/0/content_files/file12/15.pdf |title=Child marriage |publisher=Goss-online.org |access-date=2013-12-03 |archive-url=https://swap.stanford.edu/20130912135220/http://www.goss-online.org/magnoliaPublic/en/Laws--Legislation--Policies/mainColumnParagraphs/0/content_files/file12/15.pdf |archive-date=12 September 2013 }}</ref> [[Child marriage]] is common in the country, and this often leads to [[child sexual abuse]];<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2013/06/14/q-child-marriage-and-violations-girls-rights |title=Q & A: Child Marriage and Violations of Girls' Rights &#124; Human Rights Watch |publisher=Hrw.org |date=14 June 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hrw.org/news/2013/06/13/south-sudan-ending-child-marriage-will-require-comprehensive-approach |title=In South Sudan, Ending Child Marriage Will Require a Comprehensive Approach &#124; Human Rights Watch |publisher=Hrw.org |date=13 June 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> while the law on rape sets an age of consent of 18, this does not apply inside marriage. The Criminal Code criminalizes, among other behaviours, adultery and homosexuality.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.goss-online.org/magnoliaPublic/en/Laws--Legislation--Policies/mainColumnParagraphs/0/content_files/file12/15.pdf |title=The Penal Code Act, 2008 |publisher=Goss-online.org |access-date=2013-12-04 |archive-url=https://swap.stanford.edu/20130912135220/http://www.goss-online.org/magnoliaPublic/en/Laws--Legislation--Policies/mainColumnParagraphs/0/content_files/file12/15.pdf |archive-date=12 September 2013 }}</ref>
Amnesty International has stated that the security forces in South Sudan have shot and raped civilians while carrying out a civilian disarmament campaign in [[Jonglei State]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/news/south-sudan-army-and-police-forces-shooting-and-raping-civilians-jonglei-2012-10-03 |title=South Sudan: Army and police forces shooting and raping civilians in Jonglei &#124; Amnesty International |publisher=Amnesty.org |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

=== South Korea ===
In recent years, changes have been made to update South Korea's sex crime laws at the behest of President [[Park Geun-hye|Park Geun-Hye]], resulting in an increase in reported incidents. In 2015, reports of sexual assaults against foreigners were up 40% over 2008 numbers. Reports, apprehensions, and prosecutions have all risen with recent changes.<ref>{{Cite web|title = South Korea 2015 Crime and Safety Report|url = https://www.osac.gov/pages/ContentReportDetails.aspx?cid=17513|website = www.osac.gov|access-date = 18 October 2015}}</ref> However, victims often experience stigma due to traditional views of [[Women in South Korea|women]]'s place in society and, although if convicted of rape an offender may be sentenced to between seven years and life in prison, convictions seldom result in a prison sentence.<ref>{{Cite news|title = South Korea Struggles to Confront Stigma of Sexual Assaults|url = https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052702304682504579154571193810410|newspaper = The Wall Street Journal|access-date = 18 October 2015|issn = 0099-9660|first = Jason|last = Strother}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title = Raped and alone in a foreign land|url = http://www.koreaherald.com/view.php?ud=20130423001036|website = www.koreaherald.com|access-date = 18 October 2015|date = 23 April 2013}}</ref>

===Sri Lanka===
In [[Sri Lanka]] there have been recent allegations that rape and [[torture]] by the Sri Lankan security forces have continued for years after the [[Sri Lankan civil war|civil war]] ended.<ref>{{cite news|last=Harrison |first=Frances |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-asia-24849699 |title='Tamils still being raped and tortured' in Sri Lanka |work=BBC News |date=9 November 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> An average rape case in Sri Lanka takes 6 to 12 years to be resolved.<ref>{{cite web|author=Foreign & Commonwealth Office |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/news/foreign-secretary-speech-preventing-sexual-violence-in-sri-lanka |title=Foreign Secretary speech: Preventing sexual violence in Sri Lanka - Press releases |publisher=GOV.UK |date=13 November 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

The UN Multi-country Study on Men and Violence found that 14.5% of the sample of Sri Lankan men had perpetrated rape at some point in their lives. 4.9% had raped in the past year. 2.7% had raped another man. 1.6% had taken part in a gang rape. 96.5% of the men who had raped experienced no legal consequences. 65.8% did not feel worried or guilty afterwards. 64.9% of rapists had raped more than once, and 11.1% had raped four or more girls or women.<ref name="unwomen-asiapacific.org"/>

===Sudan===
The law on rape states that: "There shall be deemed to commit the offence of rape, whoever makes sexual intercourse, by way of adultery, or sodomy, with any person without his consent".<ref name="redress.org">{{cite web |title=REFORMING SUDAN'S LEGISLATION ON RAPE AND SEXUAL VIOLENCE |url=http://www.redress.org/downloads/country-reports/Position%20Paper%20Rape%205%20SEPT%2008%20_3_.pdf |website=REDRESS |access-date=10 October 2018 |date=September 2008}}</ref>

Rape and other forms of sexual violence have been reported as being used on a large scale as a weapon of war in [[Darfur]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/afr54/076/2004/en/ |access-date=18 March 2014 |title=Sudan, Darfur: Rape as a weapon of war |date=18 July 2004 }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/3549325.stm |work=BBC News |title=Mass rape atrocity in west Sudan |date=19 March 2004}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/africa/7333844.stm |work=BBC News |first=James |last=Read |title=Darfur women still face rape risk |date=7 April 2008}}</ref>

===Sweden===
{{Main|Rape in Sweden}}

A frequently cited source when comparing Swedish rape statistics internationally is the regularly published report by the [[United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime]] (UNODC), based on official statistics provided by each member state.<ref group=note>For example, see Table 3.1 (Kelly et al., 2009)</ref> In 2012, Sweden had 66 cases of reported rapes per 100,000 population, according to the [[Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention]] (Brå).<ref>{{cite web|title=Anmälda brott, totalt och per 100 000 av medelfolkmängden, efter brottstyp och månad för anmälan, år 2012 samt jämförelse med föregående år |url=http://www.bra.se/download/18.22a7170813a0d141d21800061146/1364311914171/100La-2012.xls |publisher=[[Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention]] |access-date=11 July 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140714125901/http://www.bra.se/download/18.22a7170813a0d141d21800061146/1364311914171/100La-2012.xls |archive-date=14 July 2014}}</ref> This was unequivocally the biggest number reported to the UNODC in 2012.<ref name=UNODC2013>{{cite web|title=Rape at the national level, number of police-recorded offences|url=http://www.unodc.org/documents/data-and-analysis/statistics/crime/CTS2013_SexualViolence.xls|publisher=[[UNODC]]|access-date=10 June 2014|year=2013|quote=Please note that when using the figures, any cross-national comparisons should be conducted with caution because of the differences that exist between the legal definitions of offences in countries, or the different methods of offence counting and recording.}}</ref> However, widely differing legal systems, offence definitions, terminological variations, recording practices and statistical conventions makes any cross-national comparison on rape statistics difficult,<ref name="BBC1">{{Cite news|last=Ruth|first=Alexander|title=Sweden's rape rate under the spotlight|journal=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/magazine-19592372|access-date=29 April 2014|date=14 September 2012}}</ref><ref name="BRA">{{cite web|url=https://www.bra.se/bra/bra-in-english/home/news-from-bra/archive/news/2011-01-18-how-common-is-rape-in-sweden-compared-to-other-european-countries.html|title=How common is rape in Sweden compared to other European countries?|publisher=The [[Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention]]|access-date=14 May 2014|date=18 January 2011|archive-date=22 March 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170322132203/https://www.bra.se/bra/bra-in-english/home/news-from-bra/archive/news/2011-01-18-how-common-is-rape-in-sweden-compared-to-other-european-countries.html}}</ref><ref name=statistics-caution>{{cite book|url=http://kunskapsbanken.nck.uu.se/nckkb/nck/publik/fil/visa/197/different|author1=Jo Lovett|author2=Liz Kelly|title=Different systems, similar outcomes?|date=2009|publisher=London Metropolitan University|isbn=978-0-9544803-9-4|page=17|access-date=10 July 2014}}</ref><ref name="VonHofer" /> which is why the UNODC itself cautions against using their figures.<ref name="UNODC2013" /> It should also be noted that many countries do not report any rape statistics at all to the UNODC,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Masri|first1=Mona|title=Att tolka statistik|url=http://www.sydsvenskan.se/kultur--nojen/att-tolka-statistik/|newspaper=[[Sydsvenskan]]|access-date=11 July 2014|language=sv}}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref> and some report very low numbers, despite studies that indicate otherwise.<ref>{{Cite news|title=Almost a quarter of men 'admit to rape in parts of Asia'|journal=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/health-24021573|access-date=11 July 2014|date=10 September 2013|last1=Mazumdar|first1=Tulip}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1016/S2214-109X(13)70069-X |pmid=25104346 |title=Prevalence of and factors associated with non-partner rape perpetration: Findings from the UN Multi-country Cross-sectional Study on Men and Violence in Asia and the Pacific |journal=The Lancet Global Health |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=e208–e218 |year=2013 |last1=Jewkes |first1=Rachel |last2=Fulu |first2=Emma |last3=Roselli |first3=Tim |last4=Garcia-Moreno |first4=Claudia |author5=UN Multi-country Cross-sectional Study on Men Violence research team |doi-access=free }}</ref>

[[File:Rape rate per 100,000 - country comparison - United Nations 2012.png|right|thumb|300px|Comparison of selected countries' reported rape rates, 2012]]

The Swedish police record each instance of sexual violence in every case separately, leading to an inflated number of cases compared to other countries.<ref name="BBC1" /><ref name=VonHofer>{{cite journal|title=Crime Statistics as Constructs: The Case of Swedish Rape Statistics|last1=Von Hofer|first1=Hanns|journal=European Journal on Criminal Policy and Research|date=2000|volume=8|issue=1|pages=77–89|doi=10.1023/A:1008713631586|s2cid=195221128}}</ref><ref name="method">{{cite web|title=Rape and Human Rights in the Nordic Countries |url=http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |publisher=[[Amnesty International]] |access-date=14 May 2014 |page=145 |date=2008 |quote=The Swedish mode of recording is sometimes referred to as 'extensive counting', since the crime statistics cover reported acts of rape. If a woman reports that she was subjected to several rapes by a group of men, or to repeated rapes on different occasions by one and the same man, each rape will be registered as a separate offence in the Swedish crime statistics. Furthermore, if a woman is subjected to repeated rapes during the same day by the same perpetrator, this may be registered as one or several crimes, depending on whether it is possible to distinguish each separate act. |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131020202147/http://www.amnesty.dk/sites/default/files/mediafiles/44/case-closed.pdf |archive-date=20 October 2013 }}</ref> Sweden also has a comparatively wide [[Rape in Sweden#Legislation|definition of rape]].<ref name="BBC1" /><ref name="BRA" /><ref name="statistics-caution" /> This means that more sexual crimes are registered as rape than in most other countries.<ref name="BRA" /> For example, in 2005 Sweden reformed its sex crime legislation and made the legal definition of rape much wider,<ref name="BBC1" /><ref name="paradox">{{Cite news|last=Nordlander|first=Jenny|title=Fler brott bedöms som våldtäkt|journal=Dagens Nyheter|url=http://www.dn.se/nyheter/sverige/fler-brott-bedoms-som-valdtakt/|access-date=14 May 2014|language=sv|date=10 June 2010}}</ref><ref name="explinationofthelaw">{{cite web|title=Sexualbrottslagstiftningen|url=http://www.nck.uu.se/Kunskapscentrum/Kunskapsbanken/amnen/Sexuellt_vald/Sexualbrottslagstiftningen/|publisher=[[Uppsala University]]|access-date=15 May 2014|language=sv|quote=Begreppet våldtäkt [har] blivit könsneutralt och utvidgats så att det utöver samlag även innefattar annan jämförbar handling med en person som är oförmögen att lämna sitt samtycke. [...] Efter en lagändring 1 april 2005 är det numera lika allvarligt att förgripa sig på en person som på egen hand har druckit sig kraftigt berusad som på en nykter person. Från och med 1 juli 2013 skärptes sexualbrottslagstiftningen [och] utvidgades till att omfatta de fall där offret reagerar med passivitet.|archive-date=17 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140517122507/http://www.nck.uu.se/Kunskapscentrum/Kunskapsbanken/amnen/Sexuellt_vald/Sexualbrottslagstiftningen/}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Våldtäktsbegreppet vidgas i förslag|url=http://www.sydsvenskan.se/sverige/valdtaktsbegreppet-vidgas-i-forslag/|newspaper=[[Sydsvenskan]]|access-date=14 May 2014|language=sv|date=23 April 2005|archive-date=15 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140515141111/http://www.sydsvenskan.se/sverige/valdtaktsbegreppet-vidgas-i-forslag/}}</ref> which led to a marked increase in reports.<ref name="increase">{{cite web|title=Våldtäkt och sexualbrott|url=https://www.bra.se/bra/brott-och-statistik/valdtakt-och-sexualbrott.html|publisher=[[Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention]]|access-date=15 May 2014|language=sv|quote=Sett till en tioårsperiod (2004–2013) har de anmälda våldtäkterna ökat markant, vilket till stor del kan förklaras av förändringar i sexualbrottslagstiftningen som trädde i kraft den 1 april 2005.|archive-url=https://archive.today/20170221212501/https://www.bra.se/bra/brott-och-statistik/valdtakt-och-sexualbrott.html|archive-date=21 February 2017}}</ref><ref name=reform-effort>{{cite book|url=http://kunskapsbanken.nck.uu.se/nckkb/nck/publik/fil/visa/197/different|author1=Jo Lovett|author2=Liz Kelly|title=Different systems, similar outcomes?|date=2009|publisher=London Metropolitan University|isbn=978-0-9544803-9-4|pages=9, 95, 105|access-date=10 July 2014|quote=In Sweden, reforms in 2005, which re-defined the sexual exploitation of a person in a helpless state as rape, also coincided with a marked increase in reports. [...] An expert centre for the care of battered and raped women was established, with government funding, at Uppsala University Hospital in 1995. The legal definition of rape in Sweden has been successively broadened over the last two or more decades. [...] Sweden [has] trained male and female officers in most areas}}</ref> Additionally, the Swedish police have improved the handling of rape cases, in an effort to decrease the number of [[Under-reporting|unreported cases]].<ref name="BBC1" /><ref name="reform-effort" /><ref>{{cite web|title=Viktigt att våldtäktsoffer blir trodda|date=16 June 2007 |url=http://polistidningen.se/2007/06/viktigt-att-valdtaktsoffer-blir-trodda/|publisher=Polistidningen|access-date=14 May 2014|language=sv}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Kunskapsbank - Nationellt Centrum för Kvinnofrid|url=http://www.nck.uu.se/Kunskapscentrum/Kunskapsbanken/Myndigheter/Myndighetspublikationer/?id=31|publisher=[[Uppsala University]]|access-date=14 May 2014|language=sv|quote=Insatserna från Rikspolisstyrelsen består bland annat av utbildning, informationsspridning och andra åtgärder för att förstärka Polisens förmåga upptäcka och utreda dessa brott. En annan målsättning är att allmänhetens förtroende för Polisen ska stärkas, så att fler brott anmäls.|archive-date=17 May 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140517122111/http://www.nck.uu.se/Kunskapscentrum/Kunskapsbanken/Myndigheter/Myndighetspublikationer/?id=31}}</ref> For this reason, large-scale [[Victim study|victimization surveys]] have been presented by [[Criminology|criminologists]] as a more reliable indicator of rape prevalence.<ref name="BBC1" /><ref name="BRA" /><ref name="statistics-caution" /> An EU-wide survey on sexual violence against women, published by the [[Fundamental Rights Agency|European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights]] (FRA) in 2014, showed Sweden was only third highest, below Denmark and Finland<ref name="equality">{{cite web|url=http://fra.europa.eu/sites/default/files/fra-2014-vaw-survey-main-results_en.pdf|title=Violence against women: an EU-wide survey|publisher=European Union Agency for Fundamental Rights|access-date=14 May 2014|page=28|quote=Increased gender equality leads to higher levels of disclosure about violence against women|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140307224554/http://fra.europa.eu/sites/default/files/fra-2014-vaw-survey-main-results_en.pdf|archive-date=7 March 2014}}</ref> and a previous assessment by Brå have placed Sweden at an average level among European nations.<ref name="BRA" />

According to the FRA study there is a strong correlation between higher levels of [[gender equality]] and disclosure of sexual violence.<ref name="equality" /> This, and a greater willingness among Swedish women to report rape in relationships,<ref>{{Cite news|title=Flest våldtäkter i Sverige|journal=Dagens Nyheter|url=http://www.dn.se/nyheter/sverige/flest-valdtakter-i-sverige/|access-date=14 May 2014|language=sv|date=27 April 2009|quote=[I Sverige finns] bättre anmälningsupptagning än på andra håll, våldtäktsbegreppet har utvidgats och det finns en större vilja hos svenska kvinnor att anmäla våldtäkter även inom relationer, [...] säger professor Kelly.|last1=Tures/Tt|first1=Ewa}}</ref> may also explain the relatively high rates of reported rape in Sweden, which has a long-standing tradition of gender equality policy and legislation, as well as an established women's movement,<ref name="statistics-caution" /> and has been ranked as the number one country in sex equality.<ref name="VonHofer" /><ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/business/6167486.stm |work=BBC News |title=Nordics show way in sex equality |date=21 November 2006}}</ref>

===Syria===
The [[Syrian Civil War]] has been associated with a high incidence of [[war rape]], which has led to the stigmatization of victims by their relatives and communities, and in turn to honour killings, forced marriages, and child marriages.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.trust.org/item/20131204182854-8hegf/|title=Syrian war causing 'honour killings', child marriages - doctor|work=Trust.org|access-date=18 March 2017|archive-date=27 February 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150227185441/http://www.trust.org/item/20131204182854-8hegf/}}</ref> According to the Euro Mediterranean Human Rights Network (EMHRN), about 6,000 women have been raped since the start of the conflict.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-25100122|title=Syria conflict: Women 'targets of abuse and torture'|journal=BBC News|date=26 November 2013|access-date=18 March 2017}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Nasar |first1=Sema |title=Violence against Women, Bleeding Wound in the Syrian Conflict |url=http://www.euromedrights.org/eng/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Doc-report-VAW-Syria.pdf |publisher=Euro-Mediterranean Human Rights Network |access-date=10 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140328000723/http://www.euromedrights.org/eng/wp-content/uploads/2013/11/Doc-report-VAW-Syria.pdf |archive-date=28 March 2014 |date=November 2013}}</ref>

===Tanzania===
In a survey of 1004 women (defined as 12 or older), 20% reported being raped in their lifetimes. 10% reported the event to police. In 92.4% of the events the perpetrator was known to the victim. There was no statistically significant difference between the rate of rape for women living in urban or suburban areas. 7% of the sample reported a rape occurring in the past two years. The socially closer the perpetrator, the lesser was the frequency of disclosure to either legal organs or other people, and vice versa.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.bioline.org.br/request?rh04048 |title=Bioline International Official Site (site up-dated regularly) |publisher=Bioline.org.br |date=29 November 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> The prevalence of forced sexual initiation among women varied between 14% (province) and 17% (city), according to the ''WHO Multi-country Study on Women's Health and Domestic Violence against Women''.<ref name="who.int"/>

===Turkey===
In [[Turkey]] some commonly expressed views on rape were presented when individuals from various professions were asked to agree or disagree with the statement "some women deserve rape". Thirty-three to sixty-six percent of the police officers agreed with the statement as well as nearly 50% of other professional groups. The exception were the responses of psychologists about 18% and 27% of psychiatrists who agreed with the statement. Some of these suggested that "the physical appearance and behaviors of women tempt men to rape."<ref>{{citation |url =https://yunus.hacettepe.edu.tr/~tonta/courses/fall2007/sb5002/rape.pdf |title = Turkish university students' attitudes toward rape|date = 1 December 2003}}</ref>

In 2013, ''[[The Guardian]]'' reported on claims by activists for the Kurdish terrorist group the [[Kurdistan Workers' Party|PKK]] of widespread sexual abuse of prisoners allegedly used by the Turkish government to suppress dissent.<ref>{{Cite news|author=Meral Duzgun|date=10 June 2013|url=https://www.theguardian.com/global-development-professionals-network/2013/jun/10/turkey-history-sexual-violence |title=Turkey: a history of sexual violence |journal=The Guardian |access-date=3 December 2013}}</ref>

===United Kingdom===
{{Main|Sexual offences in the United Kingdom|Rape in English law}}

The [[Sexual Offences Act 2003]] (for [[England and Wales]]), the [[Sexual Offences (Scotland) Act 2009]] and the [[Sexual Offences (Northern Ireland) Order 2008]] are relevant legislative acts in the United Kingdom.

Unlike other jurisdictions, such as Australia, much of the US, and many Western countries, 'rape' in the UK is not a gender-neutral offence: it is an offence that can only be committed by a male against a person (female or male). Also the UK has not to date{{When|date=March 2017}} followed the trend in many Western countries of classifying acts other than penetration with a penis (e.g. penetration with an object, finger) as rape. These must be prosecuted under the other, equally severe, statute of assault by penetration.

The [[British Crime Survey]] 2000 found that 61,000 women were raped in England and Wales in 1999. It was also reported that approximately 754,000 women, over the age of 16, have been raped at least once in their lifetime.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Myhill|first1=Andy|last2=Allen|first2=Jonathan|date=2002|title=Rape and sexual assault of women: The extent and nature of the problem: Home Office research study 237|website=PsycEXTRA Dataset|doi=10.1037/e454842008-001}}</ref> In 2001, the BCS ([[British Crime Survey]]) found that in the previous year, 47,000 women over the age of 16 were reported to have been raped.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Walby|first1=Sylvia|last2=Allen|first2=Jonathan|date=2004|title=Domestic Violence, Sexual Assault And Stalking: Findings from The British Crime Survey|website=PsycEXTRA Dataset|doi=10.1037/e649462007-001}}</ref>

The 2006–07 Crime Survey for England and Wales (formerly the [[British Crime Survey]]) reports that 1 in every 200 women were raped in that period. It also showed that only 800 people were convicted of rape crimes that same year, meaning that less than 1 in every 100 occurrences of rape led to a conviction.<ref name="easton1">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/blogs/thereporters/markeaston/2008/07/rape_a_complex_crime.html |title=Rape: A complex crime|last=Easton|first=Mark |publisher=BBC |date=9 July 2008 |access-date=2010-12-31}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://rds.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/pdfs08/hosb0308.pdf |archive-url=http://webarchive.nationalarchives.gov.uk/20101208185558/http://rds.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/pdfs08/hosb0308.pdf |archive-date=2010-12-08 |title=Homicides, Firearm Offences and Intimate Violence –2006/07 Supplementary Volume 2 to Crime in England and Wales 2006/07 |access-date=2015-05-28}}</ref> According to the 2015 Crime Survey for England and Wales, from January 2015 to Dec 2015, there were 34,000 incidences of rape.<ref name="bcs2015">{{cite web|url=http://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/crimeandjustice/bulletins/crimeinenglandandwales/yearendingdecember2015#sexual-offences |access-date=23 December 2016 |title=Crime in England and Wales: Year ending December 2015 - Sexual offenses |date= December 2015 |publisher= [[Office for National Statistics]]}}</ref>

According to the NCPCC, 1 in 20 children have been sexually abused in the UK.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nspcc.org.uk/preventing-abuse/child-abuse-and-neglect/child-sexual-abuse/|title=Sexual abuse|last=NSPCC|website=NSPCC|access-date=2016-05-24}}</ref> 12% of boys and 3% of girls reported committing sexual violence against their partners.<ref>Christine Barter, Melanie McCarry, David Berridge and Kathy Evans (2009).[http://www.nspcc.org.uk/Inform/research/findings/partner_exploitation_and_violence_report_wdf70129.pdf ''Partner exploitation and violence in teenage intimate relationships''] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120518100219/http://www.nspcc.org.uk/Inform/research/findings/partner_exploitation_and_violence_report_wdf70129.pdf |date=18 May 2012 }} NSPCC, pp. 81 (or more)</ref> In 2013, a [[Ministry of Justice (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Justice]] report stated that only 15 per cent of victims of the most serious sexual offences reported the incident to the police.<ref>{{cite web|title=An Overview of Sexual Offending in England and Wales|url=https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/an-overview-of-sexual-offending-in-england-and-wales|publisher=[[Home Office]] & [[Ministry of Justice (United Kingdom)|Ministry of Justice]]|access-date=16 April 2015}}</ref>

A 2013 Rape Crisis survey found that one third of the 1000 women surveyed thought that if a woman did not fight back, then she could not have experienced rape. Meanwhile, 60% thought that a woman could not have experienced rape if she did not say 'no'.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/newsbeat-23973673 |title=Newsbeat - Third of women say there are varying degrees of rape |publisher=BBC |date=6 September 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref>

According to the charity Rape Crisis 85,000 women and 12,000 men are raped each year in England and Wales, and only 15% of victims chose to report the crime to police.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rapecrisis.org.uk/statistics.php|title=rape statistics}}</ref>

In the year to the end of March 2020, 58,856 cases of rape were recorded by police forces in England and Wales. These led to just 2,102 prosecutions, compared with 3,043 in the previous 12 months.<ref>{{Cite news|date=2021-06-18|title=Why are rape prosecutions falling?|language=en-GB|work=BBC News|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-48095118|access-date=2021-08-25}}</ref>
