===United States===
{{more citations needed section|date=April 2015}}

{{Main|Rape in the United States}}

[[File:Rapes per 1000 people 1973-2003.jpg|right|thumb|300px|Rape rates in the U.S. per 1,000 people, 1973–2003]]
In 2011, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) found that "nearly 20% of all women" in the [[United States]] suffered attempted rape or rape sometime in their lives. More than a third of the victims were raped before the age of 18.<ref name="CDC">{{cite news |date=15 December 2011 |title=Nearly 97% of women in the US are raped or suffer attempted rape at some point in their lives, a US study says. |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-us-canada-16192494 |access-date=15 December 2011 |newspaper=BBC World}}</ref><ref name="NISVS2010">{{cite web |title=National Intimate Partner and Sexual Violence Survey 2010 Summary Report |url=https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/nisvs_report2010-a.pdf |access-date=16 August 2016 |publisher=Centers for Disease Control and Prevention}}</ref>

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention maintains recent statistics and standardized definitions upon which their statistics are based.<ref name="cdcstats">{{cite web | url = https://www.cdc.gov/violenceprevention/pdf/sv_surveillance_definitionsl-2009-a.pdf | access-date = 6 June 2017 | date = 2014 | publisher = National Center for Injury Prevention and Control, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention | title = Sexual Violence Surveillance: Uniform Definitions and Recommended Data Elements, Version 2.0. | last1 = Basile | first1 = KC | last2 = Smith | first2 = SG | last3 =  Breiding | first3 = MJ | last4 = Black | first4 =  MC | last5 = Mahendra | first5 =RR }}</ref>  A 2011 report on [[prison rape in the United States]] stated that "in 2008 there were at least 69,800 inmates who were raped under conditions involving force or threat of force, and more than 216,600 total victims of sexual abuse, in America's prisons, jails, and juvenile detention centers."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://ojp.gov/programs/pdfs/prea_nprm_iria.pdf|title=United States Department of Justice Initial Regulatory Impact Analysis for Notice of Proposed Rulemaking Proposed National Stand}}</ref>

Data on the prevalence of rape vary greatly depending on what definition of rape is used. The FBI recorded 85,593 rapes in 2010. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported nearly 1.3 million incidents that year. It should however be noted that the CDC's definition of rape "represents the public health perspective" and takes into account the ability of the victim to consent to sex because he or she had been drinking or taking drugs while the FBI defines rape as "Penetration, no matter how slight, of the vagina or anus with any body part or object, or oral penetration by a sex organ of another person, without the consent of the victim."<ref name="huffpost" />

A 2007 survey by the [[National Institute of Justice]] found that 19.0% of college women and 6.1% of college men experienced either sexual assault or attempted sexual assault since entering college.<ref name=":1">{{cite web|url=https://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/nij/grants/221153.pdf|title=The Campus Sexual Assault (CSA) Study|last2=Lindquist|first2=Christine H.|date=December 2007|publisher=National Institute of Justice|last3=Warner|first3=Tara D.|last4=Fisher|first4=Bonnie S.|last5=Martin|first5=Sandra L.|last1=Krebs|first1=Christopher P.}}</ref> In the ''[[University of Pennsylvania Law Review]]'' in 2017, D. Tuerkheimer reviewed the literature on rape allegations, and reported on the problems surrounding the credibility of rape victims, and how that relates to false rape accusations. She pointed to national survey data from the [[Centers for Disease Control and Prevention]] that indicates 1 in every 5 women (and 1 in 71 men) will be raped during their lifetime at some point. Despite the prevalence of rape and the fact that false rape allegations are rare, Tuerkheimer reported that law enforcement officers often default to disbelief about an alleged rape. This documented prejudice leads to reduced investigation and criminal justice outcomes that are faulty compared to other crimes. Tuerkheimer says that women face "credibility discounts" at all stages of the justice system, including from police, jurors, judges, and prosecutors. These credibility discounts are especially pronounced when the victim is acquainted with the accuser, and the vast majority of rapes fall into this category.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Deborah|first=Tuerkheimer|date=2017|title=Incredible Women: Sexual Violence and the Credibility Discount|url=http://scholarship.law.upenn.edu/penn_law_review/vol166/iss1/1/|journal=University of Pennsylvania Law Review|language=en|volume=166|issue=1}}</ref> The [[United States Department of Justice|U.S. Department of Justice]] estimated from 2005 to 2007 that about 2% of victims who were raped while incapacitated (from drugs, alcohol, or other reasons) reported the rape to the police, compared to 13% of victims who experienced physically forced sexual assault.<ref name=":1" />

The 1998 National Violence Against Women Survey, based on a sample size of 8,000, estimated the incidence of rape to be 1 in 6 for women and 1 in 33 for men, based on reports of attempted or completed rapes over the course of her or his lifetime.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles/172837.pdf|title=Prevalence, Incidence, and Consequences of Violence Against Women: Findings of the National Violence Against Women Survey|date=November 1998|publisher=National Institute of Justice|access-date=2014-02-01}}</ref>

A 1997 study on the non-institutionalized, non-military population by the U.S. [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]], which defines rape as forced penetration by the offender,<ref>Bureau of Justice Statistics, [http://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=tp&tid=317#terms_def Terms and Definitions]</ref> found that 91% of reported rape victims are female and 9% are male.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/SOO.PDF|title=Pages 5 and 8|publisher=Bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov|access-date=2013-12-03|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130305070553/http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/pdf/soo.pdf|archive-date=5 March 2013}}</ref>

The majority of rapes in the United States go unreported.<ref>{{cite web|title=Reporting of Sexual Violence Incidents|url=http://www.nij.gov/topics/crime/rape-sexual-violence/pages/rape-notification.aspx|work=[[National Institute of Justice]]|access-date=7 June 2016}}</ref><ref name="huffpost">{{Cite news|last1=Thomas|first1=Emily|title=Rape Is Grossly Underreported In The U.S., Study Finds|journal=The Huffington Post|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/2013/11/21/rape-study-report-america-us_n_4310765.html|access-date=7 June 2016|date=21 November 2013}}</ref> According to the [[American Medical Association]] (1995), sexual violence, and rape in particular, is considered the most [[Under-reporting|under-reported]] violent crime.<ref>American Medical Association (1995) Sexual Assault in America. AMA.</ref> The US Bureau of Justice Criminal Victimization Statistics reports that up to 66.1% of rapes go unreported.<ref>{{cite web|title=US Bureau of Justice Criminal Victimization Statistics, 2019 |url=https://www.bjs.gov/index.cfm?ty=pbdetail&iid=7046|website=www.bjs.gov|publisher=US Bureau of Justice|date=September 2020|access-date=8 December 2020}}</ref>  Some of the most common reasons given by victims for not reporting rapes are when the victim considers it a personal or private matter, and the fear of [[reprisal]] from the assailant.<ref name="rds.homeoffice.gov.uk">{{cite web|url=http://rds.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/pdfs05/hors293.pdf |title= A gap or a chasm? Attrition in reported rape cases |last1= Kelly |first1=L. |last2=Lovett |first2=J. |last3=Regan |first3=L.| publisher=Home Office, Home Office Research Study 293 |date=February 2005|access-date=2016-12-23 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100704220032/http://rds.homeoffice.gov.uk/rds/pdfs05/hors293.pdf |archive-date=4 July 2010}}</ref> Under-reporting affects the accuracy of this data.

A significant number of rapes reported to the police do not advance to prosecution.<ref name="Haws">{{cite journal|last=Haws |first=D |title=The Elusive Numbers on False Rape |journal=[[Columbia Journalism Review]] |year=1997 |volume=36 |issue=4 |pages=16–7 |url=http://backissues.cjrarchives.org/year/97/6/rape.asp |url-status=usurped |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080303044145/http://backissues.cjrarchives.org/year/97/6/rape.asp |archive-date=3 March 2008}}</ref> Twenty-five percent of reported rapes result in arrest.<ref>{{cite news|author=Armen Keteiyan |url=http://www.cbsnews.com/2100-500690_162-5590118.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120722025838/http://www.cbsnews.com/2100-500690_162-5590118.html |archive-date=22 July 2012 |title=Rape in America: Justice Denied |publisher=CBS News |date=9 November 2009 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> Only 16% of rapes and sexual assaults are reported to the police (Rape in America: A Report to the Nation. 1992 and United Nations Populations Fund, 2000a).<ref>{{cite web|author=Daryl C. DuLong |url=http://sa.rochester.edu/masa/stats.php |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070718110210/http://sa.rochester.edu/masa/stats.php |archive-date=18 July 2007 |title=Sexual Assault Statistics |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author1=Andrea Parrot|author2=Nina Cummings|title=Forsaken females: the global brutalization of women|url=https://archive.org/details/forsakenfemalesg0000parr|url-access=registration|access-date=1 October 2011|year=2006|publisher=Rowman & Littlefield|isbn=978-0-7425-4579-3|pages=[https://archive.org/details/forsakenfemalesg0000parr/page/n60 43]–}}</ref> Factoring in unreported rapes, about 5% of rapists will ever spend a day in jail.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ncpa.org/pdfs/st229.pdf |title=Crime & Punishment '98 .pm2 |access-date=2010-12-31 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120307125440/http://www.ncpa.org/pdfs/st229.pdf |archive-date=2012-03-07}}</ref>

[[List of common misconceptions|Contrary to widespread belief]], rape outdoors is rare. Over two thirds of all rapes occur in someone's home. 31% occur in the perpetrators' homes, 27% in the victims' homes and 10% in homes shared by the victim and perpetrator. 7% occur at parties, 7% in vehicles, 4% outdoors and 2% in bars.<ref name="Abbey">Abbey, A., BeShears, R., Clinton-Sherrod, A. M., & McAuslan, P. (2004). ''Psychology of Women Quarterly'', 28, 323–332.[http://www.hawaii.edu/hivandaids/Similarities_And_Differences_In_Women_s_Sexual_Assault_Experiences_Based_On_Tactics.pdf "Similarities and differences in women's sexual assault experiences based on tactics used by the perpetrator"] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130108020408/http://www.hawaii.edu/hivandaids/Similarities_And_Differences_In_Women_s_Sexual_Assault_Experiences_Based_On_Tactics.pdf |date=8 January 2013 }}. Accessed 9 July 2008.</ref> From 2000 to 2005, 59% of rapes were not reported to law enforcement.<ref name="rainn" /><ref name="usdoj2000">{{cite web|last1=Tjaden |first1=P |last2=Thoennes |first2=N.|title=Extent, nature, and consequences of intimate partner violence: findings from the National Violence Against Women Survey. Washington (DC)|publisher=Department of Justice (US)|year=2000|url=http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/nij/pubs-sum/181867.htm|access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref> One factor relating to this is the misconception that most rapes are committed by strangers.<ref name="rainn" /><ref name="ncjrs">{{cite web|url=http://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/ovw/206554.pdf |title=National Criminal Justice Reference Service |publisher=Ncjrs.gov |access-date=2013-12-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110708172707/http://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/ovw/206554.pdf|archive-date=2011-07-08}}</ref> In reality, studies indicate the following varying numbers:

|}

In a 2012 news story, ''The New York Times'' reported, "according to a survey by the [[Alaska Federation of Natives]], the rate of sexual violence in rural villages like Emmonak is as much as 12 times the national rate. And interviews with [[Native Americans in the United States|Native American]] women here and across the nation's tribal reservations suggest an even grimmer reality: They say few, if any, female relatives or close friends have escaped sexual violence."<ref>"[https://www.nytimes.com/2012/05/23/us/native-americans-struggle-with-high-rate-of-rape.html?_r=2&hpw For Native American Women, Scourge of Rape, Rare Justice]", ''The New York Times'', 22 May 2012.</ref> In a national survey conducted in the [[United States of America]], 14.8% of women over 17 years of age reported having been raped in their lifetime (with an additional 2.8% having experienced [[attempted rape]]) and 0.3% of the sample reported having been raped in the previous year.<ref>Tjaden P, Thoennes N. Full report of the prevalence, incidence and consequences of [https://www.ojp.gov/ncjrs/virtual-library/abstracts/extent-nature-and-consequences-rape-victimization-findings-national violence against women]: findings from the National Violence Against Women Survey. Washington, DC, National Institute of Justice, Office of Justice Programs, United States Department of Justice and Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2000 (NCJ 183781).</ref>

Drug use, especially alcohol, is frequently involved in rape. A study (only of rape victims that were female and reachable by phone) reported detailed findings related to tactics. In 47% of such rapes, both the victim and the perpetrator had been drinking. In 17%, only the perpetrator had been. 7% of the time, only the victim had been drinking. Rapes where neither the victim nor the perpetrator had been drinking were 29% of all rapes.<ref name="Abbey" /> Not only has it been a factor in the rates of sexual assault on campus, but because of the prevalence, assaults are also being affected specifically by the inability to give consent when intoxicated and bystanders not knowing when to intervene due to their own intoxication or the intoxication of the victim.<ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Pugh |first1=Brandie |last2=Ningard |first2=Holly |last3=Ven |first3=Thomas Vander |last4=Butler |first4=Leah |year=2016 |title=Victim Ambiguity: Bystander Intervention and Sexual Assault in the College Drinking Scene |journal=Deviant Behavior |volume=37 |issue=4 |pages=401–418 |doi=10.1080/01639625.2015.1026777 |s2cid=147081204}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pugh |first1=Brandie |last2=Becker |first2=Patricia |date=2018-08-02 |title=Exploring Definitions and Prevalence of Verbal Sexual Coercion and Its Relationship to Consent to Unwanted Sex: Implications for Affirmative Consent Standards on College Campuses |journal=Behavioral Sciences |volume=8 |issue=8 |page=69 |doi=10.3390/bs8080069 |issn=2076-328X |pmc=6115968 |pmid=30072605 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Koss, Gidycz and Wi published a study in 1987 where they interviewed approximately 6,000 college students on 32 college campuses nationwide. They asked several questions covering a wide range of behaviours. From this study, 15% of college women answered "yes" to questions about whether they experienced something that met the definition of rape. 12% of women answered "yes" to questions about whether they experienced something that met the definition of attempted rape. Moreover, depending on the region, 2-6% of the men interviewed admitted to rape. While the study focused on female victims and male perpetrators; it did not consider rape of men or rape in LGBT relationships.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Koss|first1=M. P.|last2=Gidycz |first2=C. A. |last3=Wisniewski |first3=N.|title=The scope of rape: Incidence and prevalence of sexual aggression and victimization in a national sample of higher education students.|journal=Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology|year=1987|volume=55|issue=2|pages=162–170|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/19663776|doi=10.1037/0022-006X.55.2.162|pmid=3494755|s2cid=2814727 }}</ref>

In 1995, the CDC replicated part of this study with 8,810 students on 138 college campuses. They examined rape only, and did not look at attempted rape. They found that 20% of women and 4% of men had experienced rape in the course of her or his lifetime.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Douglas|first=K. A.|title=Results from the 1995 national college health risk behavior survey.|journal=Journal of American College Health|year=1997|volume=46|issue=2|pages=55–66|url=http://www.tandfonline.com/loi/vach20|doi=10.1080/07448489709595589|pmid=9276349|display-authors=etal|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00049859.htm|title=Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance: The National College Health Risk Behavior Survey -- United States, 1995|publisher=Centers for Disease Control|date=14 November 1997}}</ref>

In 2000, the [[National Institute of Justice]] and the [[Bureau of Justice Statistics]] published a study called "The Sexual Victimization of College Women" based on a 1996–1997 survey. The study found that 3.1% of undergraduate women reported experiencing an act that met the researchers' definition of rape or attempted rape during a 6–7-month academic year. However, of those found to have experienced completed rape, only 46.5% of the victims answered that they considered the incident to be a rape, while 48.8% did not and 4.7% were unsure. The study also found that 10.1% of college women experienced rape and 10.9% experienced attempted rape prior to entering college. Victimization of men was not considered as part of this study.<ref>{{cite web|last=Fisher|first=Bonnie|title=The Sexual Victimization of College Women|url=https://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/nij/182369.pdf|publisher=The U.S. Department of Justice}}</ref>

In a different section of the report, the authors speculated about whether statistics during an academic year generalize to an entire college experience. For a full discussion, read more on page 10 of the report, stating that "the percentage of completed or attempted rape victimization among women in higher educational institutions might climb to between one-fifth and one-quarter" and further acknowledging in the corresponding footnote, #18, that "These projections are suggestive. To assess accurately the victimization risk for women throughout a college career, longitudinal research following a cohort of female students across time is needed."

80,000 American children are known to have been sexually abused each year. But unreported cases are higher, due to the fear among children.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.aacap.org/AACAP/Families_and_Youth/Facts_for_Families/Facts_for_Families_Pages/Child_Sexual_Abuse_09.aspx |title=Child Sexual Abuse |publisher=Aacap.org |date=20 August 2013 |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref> Over ninety percent of the time, the perpetrator is someone familiar or close with the child. Sexually violent crimes targeting children involve forced sexual activities such as intercourse, masturbation, and/or other explicit contact with a minor. According to Child Protective Services, eighty percent of the time, a parent ends up being the perpetrator. Children who become victims of this crime often end up developing phobias, depression, and post-traumatic stress disorder, as well as performing poorly in school. Sexually violent crimes of all ages occur often.<ref>[https://www.rainn.org/statistics/victims-sexual-violence Victims of Sexual Violence: Statistics] The National Crime Victimization Survey.RAINN.2016. Web 14 July 2017</ref>

According to [[United States Department of Justice]] document ''Criminal Victimization in the United States'', there were overall 191,670 victims of rape or sexual assault reported in 2005.<ref>{{cite web| url=http://bjs.ojp.usdoj.gov/content/pub/sheets/cvus/2005/cv0526.csv| title='''Table 26''' Number of incidents and victimizations and ratio of victimizations to incidents, by type of crime| work=Criminal Victimization in the United States - Statistical Tables| publisher=www.ojp.usdoj.gov |date=December 8, 2006| access-date=12 March 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130409234252/http://bjs.gov/content/pub/sheets/cvus/2005/cv0526.csv |archive-date=2013-04-09 |format=CSV}}</ref>

[[Myriam Denov]] (2004) states that societal responses to the issue of female perpetrators of sexual assault "point to a widespread denial of women as potential sexual aggressors that could work to obscure the true dimensions of the problem."<ref>Myriam S. Denov, ''Perspectives on Female Sex Offending: A Culture of Denial'' (Ashgate Publishing 2004) – ISBN.</ref> Particularly as an increasing population of un-convicted felons and rapists who continue to insist that accusation of sexual assault is a punishment in lieu of justice through law enforcement agencies. It is thought that to be accused of rape brings shame to their families and social communities.

According to the [[National Crime Victimization Survey]], the adjusted per-capita [[victimization]] rate of rape has declined from about 2.4 per 1000 people (age 12 and above) in 1980 to about 0.4 per 1000 people in 2006, a decline of about 85%.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=D'Amato |first=Anthony |title=Porn Up, Rape Down |journal=Social Science Research Network |date=23 June 2006 |ssrn=913013 }}</ref> But other government surveys, such as the Sexual Victimization of College Women study, critique the NCVS on the basis it includes only those acts perceived as crimes by the victim, and report a higher victimization rate.<ref name=FisherCullenTurner>{{cite web |last1=Fisher |first1=Bonnie S. |last2=Cullen |first2=Francis T. |last3=Turner |first3=Michael G. |url=http://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/nij/182369.pdf |title=Sexual Victimization of College Women |publisher=National Institute of Justice |date=December 2000|access-date=23 December 2016 |page=24}}</ref> Despite a decline of 60% since 1993, the US still has a relatively high rate of rape when compared to other developed countries.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.rainn.org/get-information/statistics/frequency-of-sexual-assault |title=How often does sexual assault occur? &#124; RAINN &#124; Rape, Abuse and Incest National Network |publisher=RAINN |access-date=2013-12-04}}</ref>

[[RAINN]] asserts that from 2000 to 2005, 59% of rapes were not reported to law enforcement.<ref name=rainn>{{cite web |url=http://www.rainn.org/statistics/ |title=Statistics |publisher=Rape, Abuse & Incest National Network |access-date=2008-01-01}}</ref><ref name="usdoj2000"/> For college students, the figure was 95% in 2000.<ref name=FisherCullenTurner/> One factor relating to this is the misconception that most rapes are committed by strangers.<ref>Alberto R. Gonzales et al. [http://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles1/nij/210346.pdf Extent, Nature, and Consequences of Rape Victimization: Findings From the National Violence Against Women Survey]. U.S. Department of Justice Office of Justice Programs. January 2006</ref> According to the Bureau of Justice Statistics, 38% of victims were raped by a friend or acquaintance, 28% by "an intimate" and 7% by another relative, and 26% were committed by a stranger to the victim. About four out of ten sexual assaults take place at the victim's own home.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs |title=Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) |publisher=Ojp.usdoj.gov |access-date=2013-12-04 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091211060154/http://www.ojp.usdoj.gov/bjs/ |archive-date=11 December 2009}}</ref>

===Yemen===
[[Yemen]] law does not recognize marital rape and does not provide a [[marriageable age|minimum age for marriage]]. The issues of child marriage and [[child rape]] inside marriage have made international news and have led to calls for legislative changes.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-middle-east-24083127 |title=Yemeni minister seeks law to end child marriage |work=BBC News |date=13 September 2013 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref> There have been several reports of deaths of young girls due to violent rape by adult husbands, as well as young girls dying during [[childbirth]].<ref>{{cite news|author=Mohammed Jamjoom|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2010/WORLD/meast/04/09/yemen.child.bride.death/index.html?hpt=Sbin |title=Yemeni child bride dies of internal bleeding |publisher=CNN.com |access-date=2013-12-03 |date=9 April 2010}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.news.com.au/newstest2/archive-old-assets/yemeni-child-bride-dies-of-bleeding-after-intercourse/story-e6frfkyi-1225851585843 |title=Yemeni child bride dies of bleeding after intercourse |work=News.com.au |date=8 April 2010 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|author=Mohammed Jamjoom|url=http://edition.cnn.com/2009/HEALTH/09/14/yemen.childbirth.death/index.html |title=Yemeni girl, 12, dies in painful childbirth |publisher=CNN.com |date=14 September 2009 |access-date=2013-12-03}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://edition.cnn.com/2013/09/15/world/meast/yemen-child-bride/index.html |title=Yemen minister on child marriage: Enough is enough |publisher=CNN.com |access-date=2013-12-03 |date=16 September 2013}}</ref> [[Human Rights Watch]] stated that "Child marriages and [[forced marriage]]s remain widespread, exposing young girls to [[domestic violence]] and [[maternal mortality]] and truncating their education."<ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.hrw.org/world-report-2012/world-report-2012-yemen |title=World Report 2012: Yemen &#124; |publisher=Human Rights Watch |access-date=2013-12-03|date=22 January 2012 }}</ref>
